explain: The uniform CDF is a straight line globally, but the actual positions of random keys wander around that line, and over 400,000 keys those excursions exceed 8 slots often. With a larger epsilon the wiggles fit inside the band and uniform data collapses to a single segment at eps 512. Model the data you have, not the distribution it came from.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
question: In doc-only mode, what work remains at query time?
options: Tokenizing the query and traversing the inverted index
Running the full transformer on the query
Re-encoding every candidate document
Nothing; results are precomputed per query
explain: The query is tokenized with the same vocabulary and each token gets a fixed weight (1 in SPLADE-doc, or a lookup table in OpenSearch). No transformer runs at query time.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Build it: encode, index and evaluate SPLADE on SciFact
question: You switch from one SPLADE checkpoint to another of the same size and the index doubles, while queries are unchanged. Which training choice most likely differs?
options: A weaker document-side sparsity penalty (smaller lambda_d), so documents keep more expansion terms
A larger query-side lambda_q
Integer quantization with factor 100
Max pooling instead of sum pooling
explain: Index size is total postings, which lambda_d controls through the document FLOPs term. lambda_q only shapes queries. Quantization and pooling do not double the number of non-zeros. In our run SPLADE-v3-DistilBERT and SPLADE++ ED gave 296 and 190 postings per abstract, though they also differ in size and training.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
question: Which statement about what one LambdaMART tree learns is correct?
options: It predicts each document's relevance label
It predicts NDCG for each query
It predicts the per-document lambdas from the features, pooled over all queries
It learns a separate tree for each query
explain: The regression targets are the lambdas, and Burges stresses that each tree models the lambdas for the entire dataset, not a single query. Labels enter only through |delta NDCG|.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
question: Memory holds $k_A\to4$ and $k_B\to2$ with orthogonal unit keys. A token writes $k_A\to1$ with $\beta=1$ using the delta rule. What does $k_B$ read afterwards?
explain: The update only changes $S$ along $k_A$: $S(I-k_Ak_A^\top)$ leaves the $k_B$ direction untouched because $k_A^\top k_B=0$. So $k_B$ still reads 2, while $k_A$ now reads exactly 1.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA
question: Why does GLA's chunkwise kernel need log-space arithmetic and a second level of chunks, while Mamba2's does not?
options: GLA uses softmax inside each chunk
GLA's per-channel gate products differ in every channel and underflow over a chunk, so they cannot be folded into one half-precision matmul
Mamba2 has no chunkwise form and runs only as a recurrence
GLA's state is a vector, not a matrix
explain: With a scalar gate, one ratio per token pair rescales the whole $QK^\top$ entry. With a gate per channel, each channel needs its own ratio of cumulative products, which GLA computes as exponentials of log differences in full precision, then recovers speed with sub-chunks.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
question: A shadow entry's password field is completely empty. What does that mean?
options: The account is locked
The account can log in without a password, unless the login program blocks empty passwords
The password is stored in /etc/passwd instead
The account has expired
explain: shadow(5): an empty password field means the user can log in without a password, although some programs refuse empty passwords (for example sshd with PermitEmptyPasswords no, its default). A locked account has a field starting with !.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
question: You want to stop a suspicious process but keep its memory for analysis. Which signal fits best?
options: SIGSTOP
SIGKILL
SIGTERM
SIGHUP
explain: SIGSTOP pauses the process and cannot be caught, so the program cannot react; its memory and file handles remain for inspection. SIGKILL and SIGTERM end it, and SIGHUP often just reloads configuration.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
question: What made this bug a 'regression'?
options: It only affected old 32-bit systems
It was introduced by the xz backdoor
A 2006 fix was accidentally removed during a 2020 logging rework, re-opening the same flaw
It regressed performance
explain: CVE-2006-5051 had been fixed by guarding the unsafe logging. Commit 752250c in OpenSSH 8.5p1 removed that guard while rewriting logging, so the old bug came back until 9.8p1.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: One host is a checklist, a fleet is a control loop
question: Why is idempotence the property that lets you run a hardening playbook every hour?
options: It makes the playbook run faster than a shell script
It encrypts the changes so attackers cannot see them
It guarantees the baseline itself is correct
A host already in the desired state is left unchanged, so repeated runs only fix what drifted
explain: An idempotent task checks the current state and changes only what differs. Running it again on a compliant host does nothing, which is what makes frequent enforcement safe. It says nothing about whether the baseline is a good one.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
question: Why does `SystemCallArchitectures=native` matter for a seccomp filter on x86-64?
options: It speeds up system calls
It blocks the 32-bit system call interface, whose call numbers differ, so a process cannot use that path to avoid filters written for 64-bit numbers
It disables all networking
It is required for ProtectSystem to work
explain: x86-64 Linux also accepts 32-bit system calls with a different numbering. Allowing only the native ABI closes that second door. Audit rules need the same care: rules for both arch=b64 and arch=b32 (lesson 8).

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: When audit falls behind: backlog, lost events and full disks
question: A bank's audit requirement says no security-relevant action may happen unrecorded. Which settings match that requirement, and what is the cost?
options: -f 0 and disk_full_action = ignore; no cost
-f 1 and disk_full_action = suspend; the host may halt
-f 2 and disk_full_action = halt; the host stops (panic or halt) rather than run unaudited, so a log storm becomes an outage
-e 0; audit is temporarily disabled
explain: Panic on audit failure and halt on a full disk guarantee nothing runs unrecorded, which is what the manual suggests for secure environments. The price is availability, so pair them with generous disk, rotation and alerting on space_left.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Ebury, an SSH backdoor on 400,000 servers over 15 years
question: You SSH into a suspected Ebury host and `ls -l /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils*` shows only the normal files. Why is that not reassuring?
options: Your shell was spawned by the possibly infected sshd, and Ebury's userland rootkit hooks libc in such shells to hide its files
ls cannot list symbolic links
Ebury only runs on FreeBSD
libkeyutils is not used by OpenSSH
explain: ESET documents that Ebury injects into shells spawned through the compromised OpenSSH server and hides its file, process and socket. Use systemd-run -S, a console, or an off-host check.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix
question: Why did Red Hat call the attack's noise an opportunity for defenders?
options: Because it crashes the server immediately
Because it disables logging
Because exploitation needs thousands of retries, each an unauthenticated connection timing out, which shows up as bursts of 'Timeout before authentication' in logs
Because it only works over IPv6
explain: Winning a timing race takes many attempts. Each failed attempt ends with the grace-time alarm, which sshd logs. A per-source count against a baseline catches it.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a relevance judging prompt
question: You add "You are an expert search quality rater. Ask five independent raters and average their scores" to a working judge prompt. Based on Bing's ablation, what should you expect?
options: A large gain, because personas and ensembles always help
No change, because the model ignores framing
Better agreement, but only on long documents
Possibly worse agreement: role and multiple judges each lowered kappa on average, so measure before adopting
explain: In Table 2 of Thomas et al., the role line averaged -0.04 kappa and simulated multiple judges -0.13. Effects interact (the paper notes they are not additive), which is exactly why every prompt change has to be measured against gold labels rather than assumed.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
question: Which practice from Bing's deployment directly guards against the judge drifting silently after a model update?
options: Using a role statement in the prompt
Simulating five judges per call
Weekly re-labelling of a stratified sample of recent LLM labels by trained assessors, plus a fixed query set expected not to change
Binarising grades before computing kappa
explain: Thomas et al. describe weekly stratified human re-labelling with monitoring of disagreement rates and patterns, and a large set of queries consistently re-labelled to detect any change. The other options are prompt choices, not monitoring.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
question: Model X beats model Y in 60% of head-to-head votes. Roughly how far apart are they on the Elo-style BT scale?
options: About 20 points
About 70 points
About 200 points
About 400 points
explain: The BT logit gap is ln(0.6/0.4) = 0.405. Multiplying by 400/ln 10 = 173.7 gives about 70 points. A 400-point gap would mean about a 91% win rate.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
question: Why do PII detectors combine regexes with NER models rather than use regexes alone?
options: Regexes are too slow for production
Names and addresses have no fixed format, while card numbers and emails do
NER models are always more accurate on every PII type
Regexes cannot match digits
explain: Patterns and checksums work for structured identifiers, but a person's name looks like any other word; recognizing it needs context, which is what NER models provide.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
question: A small model's forward pass takes 5 ms on the GPU, but at batch 1 the server emits a token only every 10 ms, and the GPU timeline shows gaps between steps. What helps most?
options: A GPU with twice the memory bandwidth
A larger max_num_batched_tokens
Overlapping the CPU's scheduling and output work with the GPU, and replaying the forward pass as a CUDA graph
Storing the KV cache in FP8
explain: The gaps are CPU time: scheduling, input preparation, output processing and kernel launches. More bandwidth or a smaller KV cache only shortens the 5 ms the GPU is already busy. Overlapping CPU work with the previous step and cutting launch cost removes the idle time itself.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: In the contiguous simulation, 12.8% of the pool was free yet the next request in line could not start. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Internal fragmentation
Reserved slots
Activation memory
External fragmentation
explain: Free memory existed, but not as one contiguous run long enough for the waiting request's reservation. That is external fragmentation. With fixed-size blocks any free block is usable, so external fragmentation disappears; the 0.5% left free in the paged run is just too few blocks for the next prompt.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a small engine with a block manager
question: In the engine, a step preempted a request. Why does the admission loop not run in that same step, even if blocks are free afterwards?
options: Python cannot modify the waiting deque inside a for loop
Free blocks after a preemption belong to the victim and cannot be reused
Memory just ran out, so admitting a new request would likely force another preemption soon; the freed blocks go to running requests first
Admission only runs on even steps
explain: The pool just proved too small for the running set. Admitting new work immediately would invite the next preemption and repeated recomputation. The vLLM paper and this engine admit nothing while preempted work is pending in that step.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
question: At state 6 the model's probabilities are true 0.15, false 0.34, fa 0.10, and everything else is masked. What is the masked probability of 'false'?
explain: Renormalize over the allowed set: the allowed mass is 0.15 + 0.34 + 0.10 = 0.59, and 0.34 divided by 0.59 gives 0.58. Masking never changes the ratios between legal tokens; it only removes illegal ones.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
question: A developer moves the location clauses to the top-level bool: `{"bool": {"filter": [title, seniority, skill, salary], "should": [Berlin, remote]}}`. What happens to Fay in Hamburg (not remote, salary 125k)?
options: The profile is returned: with filter clauses present, should defaults to minimum_should_match 0, so location only affects the score
The profile is excluded, because should always requires at least one clause to match
Elasticsearch rejects the query because should cannot be combined with filter
The profile is excluded, because filter clauses are evaluated after should clauses
explain: The docs state the default is 1 only when there are should clauses and no must or filter clauses. Here filter exists, so the default is 0 and the should clauses only add score. Nest the disjunction in its own bool, or set minimum_should_match explicitly.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
question: You change RankGPT's window from w=20, s=10 to w=40, s=20 at k=100, L=100. Why do input tokens fall only from 19,080 to 16,480 although calls fall from 9 to 4?
options: The larger window tokenizes more efficiently
Larger windows truncate passages
The output permutation is shorter
Passages are still read about twice, since s = w/2; only the per-window instruction and query overhead is saved
explain: Input is about 2kL plus C(I+q), where C is the number of windows. Only the C(I+q) term shrinks with fewer windows: 9 x 120 versus 4 x 120. RankGPT's own appendix (Table 12) also found larger windows did not raise nDCG@10 on DL19.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: Budget: 400 ms of model time per query, 100 retrieved candidates. Using the course model, which design fits?
options: Cross-encoder over 100, then a FIRST-style 7B on the top 20
Generated listwise with a 7B model over all 100
Pointwise 7B over all 100 on one GPU
PRP-Sliding-10 with a 7B model
explain: Cross-encoder 56 ms plus one 265 ms FIRST window is about 321 ms. The others: 10.35 s, 2.75 s and about 39.6 s.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows
question: RankGPT reranks the BM25 top 100 with w = 20 and s = 10, one pass. The 3rd most relevant passage overall sits at BM25 rank 95. If the model ranks every window perfectly, where does it end up?
options: Rank 3
Somewhere in ranks 81 to 100, because windows only reorder locally
Rank 11, the top of the second window
It is dropped from the list
explain: In every window it enters it is among the top 10 (only 2 passages anywhere beat it), so it is always carried into the next window. The 2 better passages ride up the same way, and the last window (ranks 1 to 20) sorts them exactly: rank 3. A passage outside the overall top w - s = 10 has no such guarantee.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure
question: You raise the tier-1 threshold of a two-tier cascade from 0.96 to 0.99. What happens?
options: Fewer queries escalate, so cost falls
More queries escalate: cost and mean latency rise, and accuracy usually rises because fewer weak answers are accepted
Nothing changes, since the scorer's outputs are calibrated probabilities
The weak model is skipped for hard queries, so latency falls
explain: A stricter threshold accepts fewer cheap answers, so more queries pay for the strong model and wait for both calls. The weak model still runs on every query; a cascade cannot skip it, only a router can.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Routing among many models: the cost-quality frontier
question: A new model costs 3 USD per 1,000 queries and scores 0.60 on your traffic. Your current models give a hull value of 0.67 at that cost. Which statement is right?
options: Add it as the default model, because it is cheaper than the frontier model
It can never help, so ignore it completely
It is never worth sending all traffic to, but a per-prompt router may still use it on the prompts where it beats the cheaper models
It raises the hull because it adds a new point
explain: A random mix of existing models already gets 0.67 at 3 USD, so the model alone is dominated and the hull does not move. A per-prompt router can still use it on a slice of prompts where its predicted quality per dollar is best, as the toy router used mid.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
question: Why does ORB rank FAST keypoints by the Harris measure?
options: FAST has no cornerness score and responds strongly along edges, so Harris picks the most corner-like points
Harris makes the detector scale invariant
Harris computes the orientation
Harris is needed to compute the Hamming distance
explain: The ORB paper says FAST produces no cornerness measure and has large responses along edges. Ordering by the Harris response and keeping the top N removes edge-like points. Scale comes from the pyramid and orientation from the intensity centroid.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
question: In `push`, T1's CAS fails. What does that tell T1?
options: Its node was lost and must be reallocated
Another thread's CAS on top succeeded since T1 read it, so the system made progress and T1 should relink and retry
The stack is full
A spurious failure always, because compare_exchange_weak never fails otherwise
explain: In this algorithm, top only changes through a successful CAS. If T1's CAS fails (ignoring rare spurious failures), some other push or pop completed. That is the lock-free argument in one sentence. T1's node is still private and simply gets relinked.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
question: A service uses epoch-based reclamation. One worker thread pins, then blocks on a slow network call while still pinned. What happens?
options: Nothing: EBR is lock-free
Other threads deadlock immediately
The global epoch stops advancing past one step beyond that thread's epoch, so retired memory grows without bound until it unpins
The stalled thread's reads become unsafe
explain: Advancement requires every pinned participant to be in the current epoch. The stalled thread is fine and other threads keep operating, but garbage bags can no longer age by 2 epochs, so memory grows. Keep pinned regions short and never block inside them.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
question: Your per-template counters show T2 done collapsing while T1 recv holds steady, and a brand new template T3 exc appearing. What does the pair of signals tell you that a single total-log-volume alert could not?
options: Nothing extra: total volume would have dropped too
Only that something changed, since template counts cannot be attributed to code paths
That work is still arriving but stopped completing, and a previously unseen code path is now executing, which localizes the fault to one logging statement and its callers
That the parser is drifting and the templates should be recomputed
explain: Total volume barely moves here: T1 is flat and T2's loss is partly replaced by T3's gain. Per-template series separate arrival from completion and surface the new error path. A new template id is the strongest single signal in log analytics, which is why it deserves its own first-seen rule rather than a z-score.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Log formats: syslog, JSON and Windows XML
question: Which is the PRI of a message with facility 13 (log audit) and severity 5 (Notice)?

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: SIEM queries: SQL, KQL and SPL on one toy dataset
question: Our toy query counts c7's denials in fixed 10-minute buckets with a threshold of 5. What does it report for c7?
options: One alert with 6 denials
Two alerts with 3 each
No alert: the buckets hold 3 and 3
An error, because 22:56 is not on a bucket boundary
explain: Fixed (tumbling) buckets cut the burst at 23:00, so neither bucket reaches 5. Six denials in eight minutes go unreported. Sliding windows, in lesson 14, catch it.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Detection as code: rules in git, tests and CI
question: Why should the test events and the rule live in the same repository and change in the same pull request?
options: Git cannot store JSON elsewhere
To make the SIEM faster
So a reviewer sees the logic change and the evidence it behaves as intended together, and history links them
Sigma requires it
explain: Reviewing a rule change without its tests is reviewing intent, not behaviour. Keeping them together also means reverting one reverts both.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Threat hunting and the Pyramid of Pain: the FireEye alert
question: What distinguishes threat hunting from detection?
options: Hunting uses different logs
Detection is done by people and hunting by machines
Hunting only uses threat intelligence feeds
Hunting is a human-led, hypothesis-driven search that does not wait for an alert; good hunts become detections or reveal data gaps
explain: Both use the same data. Hunting explores what rules do not yet cover; when a hunt's query proves precise enough it graduates into an automated detection.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
question: With Ring Attention on N hosts, after how many compute steps has host 0's query block seen every KV block of the sequence (one layer, forward pass)?
options: N
log2 N
N squared
explain: Each step delivers one new KV block from the predecessor. Host 0 starts with its own block and needs N - 1 more hops, so N compute steps in total (Algorithm 1 loops over the N - 1 transfers).

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
question: You convert a 12-layer model into a (1 x 12) looped model of the same width. Which statement is correct?
options: Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs stay about the same
Parameters stay the same and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Both stay the same because the unrolled graph is identical
explain: The looped model stores one block instead of twelve, so parameters drop about 12x. But each token still goes through twelve block applications, so FLOPs (and latency) are about the same. The unrolled graph has the same shape, but its weights are tied, which is exactly what removes the parameters.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
question: Using the model card's rule (materialized params = 1.5r + 2 billion), what does running Huginn at r = 16 correspond to, and how many effective layers is that?
options: 26B and 68 layers
24B and 64 layers
26B and 64 layers
50B and 132 layers
explain: 1.5 x 16 + 2 = 26 billion. Effective depth is 2 prelude + 4 x 16 core + 2 coda = 68 layers. 50B and 132 layers is the r = 32 point.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
question: An Ouro gate outputs lambda = 0.3, 0.5, 0.2 at steps 1 to 3 (T_max = 4). With threshold q = 0.7, after which step does the token exit?
options: Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4
explain: Exit-first probabilities: 0.3, then 0.5 x 0.7 = 0.35, then 0.2 x 0.35 = 0.07. Cumulative: 0.30, 0.65, 0.72. The first to reach 0.7 is step 3. Note the cumulative value, not the gate's own output, is compared with q.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Build it: a LoRA layer from scratch, then the same run with PEFT
question: A teammate's LoRALinear has no merged flag: forward always returns `base(x) + s * B(A(x))`. They call `merge()` before serving. What does the served layer compute?
options: W0x + 2sBAx: the update is counted twice, once in the weight and once in the adapter path
W0x + sBAx, exactly as during training
W0x only, because merge() zeroes A and B
An error, because the merged weight no longer matches A and B in shape
explain: merge() already added sBA into the base weight, so base(x) returns (W0 + sBA)x. Without the flag the adapter path adds sBAx again. That is why both our class and PEFT skip the low-rank path once a layer is merged.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: A training recipe: learning rate, rank, alpha, dropout and evaluation
question: A LoRA run on a 7B model with all activations stored runs out of memory at batch 8 and 2048-token sequences. Which change frees the most memory?
options: Lower the LoRA rank from 16 to 8
Turn on gradient checkpointing
Target only q and v instead of all linear layers
Lower lora_alpha
explain: The adapters with their gradients and Adam state take about 0.64 GB at r = 16, so halving rank or targets saves well under 1 GB. Activations at this shape are 73 to 245 GB, and checkpointing cuts what is stored to about 4.3 GB plus one layer at a time. Alpha changes no memory at all.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
question: During NPO with beta = 1, a forget example's probability is now 1% of the reference model's. Compared with plain gradient ascent, how strongly does this example still push the weights?
options: Equally strongly, NPO only changes the loss value, not the gradient
About 2% as strongly, the weight is 2(0.01)/(0.01 + 1) = 0.020
About 50% as strongly, the weight bottoms out at 0.5
Twice as strongly, because NPO doubles the gradient
explain: NPO's gradient is the GA gradient times W = 2r^b / (r^b + 1). With r = 0.01 and b = 1 that is 0.02 / 1.01, about 0.020. The weight stays near 1 only for very small beta, where NPO behaves like GA; there is no floor at 0.5, it keeps falling toward 0.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Toward robust unlearning: tamper resistance, distillation, filtering
question: Which protection did pretraining data filtering (Deep Ignorance) fail to provide on its own?
options: Resistance to thousands of steps of adversarial fine-tuning
Unchanged performance on unrelated benchmarks
Protection when the filtered information is supplied in the prompt, for example by a search tool
Low accuracy on the biothreat proxy questions before any attack
explain: Filtered models resisted up to 10,000 fine-tuning steps and kept their general capabilities, but a model can still use knowledge handed to it in context. The authors recommend defense in depth, for example adding circuit-breaking, which helped against such attacks.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Notarization, revocation and the Shlayer lesson
question: A colleague says "the installer is notarized, so it is safe to approve". What is the most accurate reply?
options: Correct: notarized apps are reviewed by Apple staff
Notarization only means an automated scan found no known malware at upload time; Shlayer was notarized twice in 2020
Notarization only applies to App Store apps
Notarization means the app is sandboxed
explain: Apple itself says notarization is not App Review. Shlayer's notarized payloads show that scanning for known malicious content misses new or disguised code.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Breaking TCC: $HOME poisoning, powerdir and XCSSET
question: Apple's fix for CVE-2020-9934 replaced `$HOME` with `getpwuid()`. Why was that not the end of the story?
options: getpwuid() is slower
getpwuid() does not work as root
It still trusted the user's directory record, and powerdir found a way to change that record's home directory
It removed the user database
explain: The fix removed one attacker-controlled input (an environment variable) but kept a dependency on the stored home directory. Microsoft changed that via dsexport/dsimport, leading to CVE-2021-30970.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Endpoint Security: the API every Mac EDR is built on
question: A vendor wants to block unknown binaries before they run. Which ES design fits?
options: Subscribe to NOTIFY_EXEC and kill the process afterwards
Use eslogger with --oslog
Load a kernel extension
Subscribe to AUTH_EXEC and answer allow or deny within the deadline
explain: Only AUTH events pause the operation for a decision. NOTIFY arrives after the fact; eslogger supports no AUTH events; kexts are deprecated and need Reduced Security on Apple silicon.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Case: Atomic Stealer and the paste-into-Terminal era
question: Why did stealer operators move from fake app DMGs to "paste this into Terminal"?
options: Terminal commands run as root automatically
DMGs no longer open on macOS
Commands typed by the user and scripts piped into osascript skip the quarantine-triggered Gatekeeper and notarization checks
Terminal disables XProtect
explain: Microsoft's analysis states it directly: scripts launched from Terminal don't undergo the Gatekeeper evaluation that app bundles opened from Finder may get, and Sequoia had made overriding Gatekeeper for apps harder.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The malware economy: loaders, access brokers and RaaS
question: Why do CISA's analysts say LockBit intrusions vary so much in technique?
options: LockBit rewrote its code for every victim
LockBit only used zero-day exploits
Different countries' laws changed the malware
Many unconnected affiliates used the same ransomware, each with their own tradecraft
explain: In RaaS the developer supplies the tools and the affiliates do the intrusion. The ransomware binary is shared; how the network is breached and explored depends on which affiliate you face.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The stack in assembly: tracing a compiled function
question: In the x86-64 trace, where did the argument len (3) arrive, and where was it stored?
options: In rdi, stored at rbp-8
On the stack only, at rbp+8
In rax, stored at rbp-4
In edx (low half of rdx, the second argument register), stored at rbp+0x18 in the shadow store
explain: Microsoft x64 passes argument 2 in rdx. The -O0 code spills it to its home slot in the caller's shadow store, rbp+0x18. rbp+8 is the return address.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Packing, obfuscation and entropy
question: Which entropy value would you expect for a section that is encrypted with a strong cipher?
options: About 0.5
Close to 8
About 3
About 5.9, like normal code
explain: Good encryption output is indistinguishable from random bytes, which approach 8 bits per byte. Normal x86 code sat at 5.88 in our sample.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
question: You truncate stored 1024-d unit vectors to 256 dims and forget to re-normalize them. Queries are truncated and re-normalized. You rank by dot product. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: re-normalizing the query is enough to restore cosine order
All scores shrink by the same factor, so the order is unchanged
Scores now mix angle with each document's prefix length, so documents with long prefixes are favored
Dot products become negative for every document
explain: Each stored prefix keeps a different share of its length (0.903 for X and 0.515 for Y in the toy). The dot product multiplies cosine by that length, so long-prefix documents get a boost unrelated to relevance. Normalizing only the query scales every score equally and cannot fix it.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Lab: when does Matryoshka training actually pay off?
question: Why did the NLI Matryoshka twin show no clear prefix advantage on SciFact, while it did on STS?
options: Its nested loss shaped the prefixes for NLI-style similarity, and SciFact asks a different question that neither NLI model answers well
Matryoshka models only work on images
SciFact abstracts are longer than 768 tokens, so the prefixes overflow
The twin was evaluated without re-normalizing its prefixes
explain: The loss keeps the training task's notion of similarity in the prefixes. On STS, the task family the pair was trained for, the twin kept 98.37% at 64 dims vs 96.46%. On out-of-domain retrieval, where both start weak (0.373 and 0.354), the prefixes kept 51.5% and 54.0%. Both runs re-normalized the prefixes.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
question: Why did Megatron adopt 1F1B (PipeDream-Flush) over GPipe even though both have the same bubble?
options: 1F1B needs no pipeline flush
1F1B sends fewer bytes between stages
1F1B caps in-flight microbatches at p instead of m, so activation memory stops growing with the number of microbatches
1F1B lets each microbatch use slightly stale weights, which is faster
explain: The bubble is (p-1)/m for both. GPipe stores activations for all m microbatches; 1F1B starts backward passes early and never has more than p outstanding. This is what makes a large m (small bubble) affordable.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Mixture of experts at scale: EP, token dispatch and parallel folding
question: Attention runs with TP = 2, CP = 2, DP = 2 on 8 GPUs. Without folding, EP must live inside the DP group. What is the largest EP without and with MoE parallel folding?
options: 2 without folding, 8 with folding
8 in both cases
4 without folding, 4 with folding
2 in both cases, since folding only changes TP
explain: Without folding the expert group is a subgroup of DP, so EP is at most DP = 2. Folding lets the MoE layers regroup all 8 GPUs (ETP x EP x EDP = 8 per pipeline stage), so EP = 8 with ETP = 1 and EDP = 1 is allowed.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: What only RAM knows: Duqu 2.0 and the case for memory
question: You image only the disk of a server where an attacker used an in-memory web shell like BEHINDER. What are you most likely to miss?
options: The implant's code and the commands it ran, because they existed only in the server process's memory
Nothing, because every web shell is written to the web root
Only the timestamps, which memory cannot hold anyway
The operating system version
explain: An in-memory implant is loaded into the running server process and never written to disk. Volexity found BEHINDER and the attacker's commands in process memory, not in files.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Inside Volatility 3: layers, symbols, templates and automagic
question: What does a translation layer do in Volatility 3?
options: Maps addresses on itself to addresses on a lower layer, for example virtual to physical by walking page tables
Converts the image to a different file format on disk
Translates plugin output into other languages
Downloads symbols from Microsoft
explain: Data layers hold bytes; translation layers map addresses onto lower layers. The Intel layer, the LiME layer and the swap layer are all translation layers.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Hollowing, reflective loading and how memory gives them away
question: A thread in lsass.exe started at an address inside a private VAD that maps no file. Which ATT&CK techniques does this fit, and what do you do next?
options: Normal LSASS start-up; no action
A disk failure; check SMART data
Process injection or reflective loading; dump the VAD, check malfind and ldrmodules for it, and look for who opened lsass with write access
Kerberos ticket renewal; check the domain controller
explain: Threads normally start in mapped image code. A start inside unbacked private memory is the footprint of injected or reflectively loaded code, and in lsass it is urgent.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Linux memory: banners, task lists, bash history and kernel checks
question: Why can linux.bash find commands that are not in the user's .bash_history file?
options: It decrypts the history file
It reads the kernel's audit log
It replays the terminal's keystrokes from the network
It reads history held in the running bash process's heap, which exists before (and even without) bash writing the file
explain: Bash keeps each shell's history in its own memory. The file on disk is a separate copy that may never have been written, or may have been deleted; memory holds the live one.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
question: A heap has 6 KiB free in six 1 KiB holes and gets a 2 KiB request. Which change would let the request succeed without growing the heap?
options: Rounding the request up to 4 KiB
Switching to a faster free-list search
Freeing one more object that sits between two holes, so they coalesce
Adding a second free list for 1 KiB holes
explain: The request fails because no two free bytes are adjacent. Freeing an object between two holes lets the allocator coalesce them into a 3 KiB hole. Search speed and extra lists do not create contiguity, and rounding up makes the request harder to fit.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
question: On an x86 machine the SB test (x = 1; r1 = y in one thread, y = 1; r2 = x in the other) sometimes ends with r1 = 0 and r2 = 0. What is the best explanation?
options: The cache coherence protocol lost one of the writes
Each core's store sat in its store buffer while the same core's later load read the old value from memory
The two threads ran on the same core, so they could not see each other
x86 reorders every pair of memory operations freely
explain: Both writes eventually reach memory, so nothing was lost. x86-TSO only allows a store to be delayed past a later load, which is exactly what the store buffer does. Threads time-sliced on one hardware thread share one store buffer, so they would not produce it (two hyperthreads of one core have separate buffers and can), and x86 does not reorder loads with loads or stores with stores.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: Code using `Relaxed` for a ready flag passes millions of test runs on x86-64 CI but corrupts data on an ARM64 server. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: ARM64 has a broken cache coherence protocol
The code was always wrong: x86-64 gives acquire/release ordering to plain loads and stores, which hid the missing Release/Acquire
x86-64 runs Relaxed operations as SeqCst, so the code is correct on x86-64 and only ARM64 needs a fix
The ARM64 compiler has a bug
explain: The memory model never promised ordering for Relaxed. x86-TSO happens to prevent the message-passing reordering, but the compiler could still reorder the operations even there. The fix is a Release store and an Acquire load, which costs nothing extra on x86-64.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
question: A request handler calls `epoch::pin()`, reads a node from a lock-free map, then makes a 2-second network call before dropping the guard. What is the main problem?
options: The node may be freed during the network call
The network call will deadlock
No memory retired by any thread during those 2 seconds can be reclaimed
The guard will be dropped automatically after 128 pins
explain: The node is safe; the guard guarantees that. The cost lands on everyone else: the pinned thread keeps the global epoch from advancing past its epoch plus one, so all garbage retired meanwhile waits. Copy what you need, drop the guard, then do the slow call.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Where things live: code, static data, heap and stack
question: A function declares `char buf[64];` inside its body and calls `malloc(64)` into `char *p`. Where do the 64 bytes behind `buf` and behind `p` live?
options: Both on the heap
Both on the stack
buf in static data; p's bytes on the stack
buf on the stack; the bytes p points to on the heap (p itself is a local on the stack)
explain: Local arrays are part of the function's stack frame. malloc returns memory from the heap; the pointer variable p is a local, so p itself sits on the stack while the 64 bytes it points to are on the heap.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Off-by-one: a single byte too far
question: Which loop writes one byte past `char a[10]`?
options: memset(a, 0, sizeof a);
explain: With <= the loop runs for i = 10 as well, and a[10] is the 11th byte of a 10-byte array. The other three touch exactly indices 0 to 9.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Format string bugs: when user text becomes instructions
question: Input `%p %p %p` printed three hex values. What were they?
options: The contents of the argument registers and stack slots where printf expected arguments, left over from earlier code
Random numbers generated by printf
The addresses of the three % signs
An error message
explain: printf fetched three pointer-sized arguments from where arguments live. Since none were passed, it read leftovers, which here included stack and library addresses. That is an information leak.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
question: Your triplet loss drops to near zero within the first epoch, but retrieval quality barely improves. What is the most likely cause?
options: The margin is too large
The learning rate is too small
Triplets are sampled at random, so almost all are easy and give no gradient
The embedding is L2-normalized
explain: Random triplets are mostly easy: the negative is already beyond d(a,p) + m, so the loss is zero regardless of how good the embedding is. A low loss here says nothing. Mine harder triplets.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: DoNotOptimize, loop hoisting and who owns the loop
question: A Google Benchmark loop does `auto h = hash(key); benchmark::DoNotOptimize(h);` where key is a std::string built once before the loop. The result looks too fast. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add benchmark::ClobberMemory() after the hash
Call DoNotOptimize on key (or its data) inside the loop as well, so the hash cannot be hoisted
Wrap the call in your own loop of 1000 and divide by 1000
Run with --benchmark_repetitions=10
explain: The output is consumed, but the input never changes, so hash(key) is loop-invariant and may be computed once. Escaping the input each iteration forces recomputation. ClobberMemory only flushes pending stores; an inner loop gives the optimizer more to merge; repetitions repeat the same wrong number.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
question: A colleague sets rollout_batch_size 16, n_samples_per_prompt 4, global_batch_size 32 and num_steps_per_rollout 3. What happens?
options: Miles trains 3 steps and discards the 16 unused samples
Miles aborts with a validation error because 64 is not equal to 96
Miles reuses 32 samples to fill the third step
Miles silently changes n_samples_per_prompt to 6
explain: 16 x 4 = 64 samples are produced, but 32 x 3 = 96 would be consumed. With all four knobs set inconsistently, the docs say Miles aborts with a validation error instead of guessing which knob you meant.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay: why experts flip and how R3 pins them
question: An MoE run uses TIS with the default interval but no R3. Which effect of a routing flip does TIS NOT undo, even when it catches the token?
options: The token's probability ratio exceeding 2
An outlier token dominating the batch gradient
The token's loss weight being larger than 2
The gradient for that token flowing into an expert that never produced it during rollout
explain: TIS clamps or drops the token's weight, which bounds its ratio and its share of the gradient. But whatever weight the token keeps, the trainer's forward pass still routed it through its own experts, so the update reaches experts rollout never used. Only replaying the routes fixes that.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
question: A 3-slot cache holds X, Y and Z. Their next requests are: X in 7 requests, Y never, Z in 2 requests. A miss for W arrives. What does Belady's MIN evict?
options: Z, because it was used least recently
X, because it is needed later than Z
Y, because it is never requested again
W is not admitted, because MIN only evicts on hits
explain: MIN evicts the object whose next request is furthest away, and never counts as furthest of all. Recency (option one) is LRU's rule, not MIN's. X is a reasonable second choice but loses to Y.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
question: Using Lykouris and Vassilvitskii's result, what happens to their predictor-augmented Marker algorithm if the oracle's predictions become arbitrarily bad?
options: It stays within O(log k) of optimal, the same bound as classic Marker without predictions
Its competitive ratio grows without bound
It becomes exactly as good as Belady's MIN
It refuses to evict
explain: The point of the construction is robustness: the ratio improves as prediction error falls, but it is always capped by O(log k), which is achievable with no oracle at all. Blindly following the oracle has no such cap.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: a test device, a proxy and the app's own files
question: In the Starbucks case, the app kept its OAuth token in the Keychain, yet the password still leaked. Which MASVS control did the app fail?
options: MASVS-STORAGE-2: the app prevents leakage of sensitive data, here through a log file
MASVS-NETWORK-1, because the password was sent in cleartext
MASVS-RESILIENCE-1, because the phone could be jailbroken
MASVS-CRYPTO-1, because the Keychain is weak
explain: Storing the token securely satisfies part of STORAGE-1, but the password reached a log through the crash reporter: a leak, which is STORAGE-2. There was no network flaw in the advisory, and resilience controls would not stop an app from writing its own log.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
question: An app's WebView exposes `addJavascriptInterface(Bridge(), 'native')` and loads only `https://help.example.com`. The help site embeds a third-party chat widget in an iframe. What can the widget's script do?
options: Call the bridge's @JavascriptInterface methods, because the object is injected into every frame, including iframes
Nothing: iframes cannot see objects added by the app
Only read the page's text
Call the bridge only if the user taps inside the iframe
explain: Android's guidance says addJavascriptInterface injects the object into every frame, including iframes, with no way to check the calling frame's origin. Third-party content on your own page therefore reaches your native code. addWebMessageListener with origin rules, or no bridge, fixes it.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Running a mobile app assessment end to end, and where to practise
question: The scope says 'profile MAS-L2+P'. During testing you find the app has no jailbreak detection and no obfuscation. How should these appear in the report?
options: As informational observations at most, since MAS-R is not in the agreed profile and their absence is not in itself a vulnerability
As high-severity findings under MASVS-STORAGE
They should not be mentioned at all
As critical, because the backend can be called directly
explain: Resilience controls belong to MAS-R. Under L2+P they are optional defence in depth, so at most an observation, perhaps with a note on when they would matter (fraud, cheating). Calling the API directly is a backend question, answered by server-side checks, not by client obfuscation.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Decoupled RoPE: why position breaks absorption
question: A colleague's absorbed MLA decoder applies RoPE at position t to the full 512-wide absorbed query, then dots it with the cached latents. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, RoPE commutes with the latent projection
It only fails for contexts longer than 4K
The rotation now acts in latent space, which does not equal rotating each head's keys; position information is wrong and the scores no longer match the trained model
The cache size doubles
explain: RoPE in MLA must only touch the decoupled 64-wide parts. The content part was trained without rotation, and a rotation applied in the 512-wide latent space is not the per-head offset rotation $R_{j-t}$ of the key, so the scores no longer match the trained model. Lesson 5 runs this exact bug.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
question: A GQA layer like those in Meta's Llama models has 32 query heads, 8 KV heads and $d_h = 128$. What latent size rewrites it exactly as MLA, and what happens to its cache?
options: 128, and the cache shrinks 16x
4,096, and the cache doubles
1,024, and the cache halves
2,048, and the cache stays the same size
explain: The latent is the stacked keys and values, $2 g d_h = 2 \times 8 \times 128 = 2048$, which is exactly what GQA already caches per token per layer. Saving memory needs a further compression step.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
question: A batch of 64 decode rows is spread across 64 different adapters. According to Punica's roofline analysis, what limits the SGMV kernel?
options: Tensor Core throughput, because there are 64 matmuls
Memory bandwidth, because each row reads its own adapter weights and does little math per byte
PCIe bandwidth (the CPU-to-GPU bus), because adapters are always loaded from the CPU
Nothing: the cost is identical to one shared adapter
explain: With n = s_n the I/O term n h_i h_o grows with the batch, so arithmetic intensity stays about 0.94 FLOPs per byte, firmly bandwidth bound. Measured latency rose from 37 to 116 microseconds, versus 37 to 40 for a single shared adapter.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model
question: Which statement about LoRAX matches its documentation?
options: It requires all adapters to be merged before serving
It only supports one adapter per GPU
It batches requests for different adapters together and swaps adapters between GPU and CPU memory
It replaces the base model with a quantized adapter
explain: LoRAX documents heterogeneous continuous batching (different adapters in one batch) and adapter exchange scheduling (prefetch and offload between GPU and CPU), using Punica's SGMV kernel.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: How N trades recall against latency and cost
question: Searches run in parallel and the LLM rewrite takes 600 ms. You raise N from 4 to 8. Which effect is largest, under the model in this lesson?
options: End-to-end latency roughly doubles
Latency and load both stay the same
Recall doubles
End-to-end latency rises a little, while retriever load and candidate count roughly double
explain: In parallel, the search phase grows with the slowest of N (about m H_N: 83 ms to 109 ms at m = 40), small next to 600 ms of LLM time. But every extra query is another search to serve and more candidates downstream, so load and context grow linearly. Recall gains shrink as N grows.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
question: Which scorer could you put directly over a 50-million-document index as the **first** stage?
options: A cross-encoder, if you batch on a large GPU
A bi-encoder or late-interaction model, because document vectors are precomputed and searchable with ANN
Only BM25; neural models cannot be first stages
duoBERT with the SAMPLE aggregation
explain: First stages need precomputed document representations so the query can be matched with an index. Bi-encoders give one vector per document; ColBERT indexes token vectors and retrieves end to end. A cross-encoder has nothing to index: it needs a forward pass per pair.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
question: During training, what does the head that predicts x(t+3) receive as input at position t?
options: The shared representation of the prefix x(1..t) only
The prefix plus head 1's and head 2's predicted tokens
The true tokens x(t+1) and x(t+2), via teacher forcing
The whole sequence, with future tokens masked out after the loss
explain: In the Gloeckle design all heads read the same shared representation of the prefix ending at t and predict in parallel. No head sees other heads' guesses or any token after t. (DeepSeek-V3 makes a different choice, covered in lesson 4.)

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Add MTP to your GPT: both designs in about 60 lines
question: Your Gloeckle-style model uses n = 4 heads with L = 6 blocks in total. How many trunk blocks does it have, and why does that matter for comparing against n = 1?
options: 2 trunk blocks plus 4 head blocks, so all models have 6 blocks and gains cannot come from extra parameters
6 trunk blocks plus 4 heads; MTP models are meant to be larger
5 trunk blocks, as for n = 1, so only the heads differ
0 trunk blocks; heads replace the trunk
explain: The trunk has L - n = 2 blocks. Adding head blocks while removing trunk blocks keeps the total at 6, matching the paper's equal-parameter comparisons. It also means a 4-head model has a much shallower shared trunk, one reason MTP can hurt small models.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
question: An update has singular values 4.00, 1.00, 0.197 and 0.0019. What does replacing it with its orthogonalized version $UV^\top$ do?
options: Shrinks every entry toward zero, like weight decay
Keeps only the top direction and discards the rest
Keeps the same singular directions but sets every singular value to 1, boosting the weak directions relative to the strong one
Makes the update elementwise plus or minus 1, exactly like sign descent
explain: $UV^\top$ keeps $U$ and $V$ (the directions) and replaces $S$ with the identity. The strongest direction is scaled down from 4.00 to 1 and the weakest is scaled up from 0.0019 to 1. Sign descent is a different, elementwise operation, and as we saw it gives singular values 3.24, 2.00, 1.24, 0.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: You need to estimate SOAP's optimizer memory for a $4096 \times 4096$ matrix, counting state plus the gradient as the paper does. Which is closest?
options: 33.6M floats, one buffer like Muon
50.3M floats, the same as AdamW
117.4M floats
281 trillion floats, like full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ with $m = n = 4096$ is $33.6 + 33.6 + 50.3 \approx 117.4$ million. AdamW uses $3mn = 50.3$M (gradient, first and second moment); Muon uses about $2mn = 33.6$M (gradient and one momentum buffer).

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
question: In the toy problem, what is the best value of the knob c when n = 4096?
options: 0.0361, the same as at n = 256
explain: $c^* = 1/\sqrt{3n} = 1/\sqrt{12288} \approx 0.00902$. The c knob shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so 16x the width gives a 4x smaller c. 0.577 is the best alpha, which is the width-independent knob.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
question: A colleague's hand-written muP uses `{'params': hidden, 'lr': lr / m}` for hidden weights and computes logits as `self.unemb(h) / m`, but initializes the unembedding with std $\sigma/\sqrt{m}$ and puts it in the hidden group. What does the coord check show?
options: Flat curves, because the 1/m factors cancel
Exploding hidden activations
Nothing; the unembedding has no width dimension
Logits whose updates shrink with width, because the output layer is scaled down twice: by the forward multiplier and again by the hidden-group LR
explain: Table 8 puts the width factor for output weights in the forward multiplier and keeps their LR and init constant. Also dividing the LR by $m$ makes the unembedding's updates, and so the logit changes, shrink like $1/m$: the output layer stops learning at large width.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
question: You tuned a muP proxy on 2B tokens and found base LR $4\times10^{-3}$. The target is the same family, 16x wider, trained for 200B tokens. Which adjustment does the evidence say you are most likely missing if you only apply muP's width rules?
options: Multiply the LR by 16 for the longer run
Nothing; muP makes the LR independent of every scale
Lower the LR for the 100x longer horizon, to roughly 0.23x by the fitted law
Double the dropout
explain: muP covers width. Bjorck et al. show the optimal LR keeps falling with the token horizon, also under muP, roughly like $D^{-0.32}$ for large models: $100^{-0.32} \approx 0.23$. Fit the exponent on two or three short horizons if you can.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
question: A thread calls lock on an unlocked three-state mutex and later unlocks it, with no other thread involved. How many system calls happen?
options: One: the wake in unlock
Two: a wait and a wake
One: the CAS is a system call
Zero
explain: The CAS turns 0 into 1 in user space. At unlock the swap returns 1, not 2, so the wake is skipped. Atomic instructions are not system calls; the kernel never sees an uncontended lock.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
question: Which change makes the doctors example safe while staying at Repeatable Read?
options: Run both transactions with a shorter timeout
Add an index on the on_call column
Lock the rows being counted, for example SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on all on-call doctors, so the second transaction waits and then fails or sees the change
Switch to Read Committed so each statement sees fresh data
explain: Write skew comes from reads that do not conflict with the other transaction's write. Turning the reads into row locks (FOR UPDATE) materializes the conflict: the second transaction blocks, then hits a concurrent update error at Repeatable Read. Read Committed does not help; both counts can still run before either update.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
question: In the CoNLL-2003 data files, when does a B-ORG tag appear?
options: Only when an organisation starts immediately after another organisation ends
At the start of every organisation entity
On every token of a multi-token organisation except the first
Only on single-token organisations
explain: The files use IOB1, the Ramshaw and Marcus scheme: entity tokens are I-ORG by default, and B-ORG marks only the leftmost token of an organisation that immediately follows another organisation. The option saying every organisation entity starts with B-ORG describes IOB2, which is what most modern pipelines convert the files to.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
question: Your log tagger scores 91 F1 on a weakly labelled held-out split and 62 F1 on 200 hand-labelled lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weakly labelled split shares the labelling functions' blind spots, so it rewards reproducing them rather than finding entities
The hand-labelled set is too small for the metric to be meaningful
The model overfitted the 200 hand-labelled lines
Entity F1 is not comparable across splits
explain: A test set built by the same regexes and gazetteers as the training labels cannot reveal what those functions miss. The tagger gets credit for imitating them. Only human labels measure the task, which is why some of your annotation budget must be held out and never used for training.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: International law in cyberspace: force, intervention and sovereignty
question: Which operation do the UK Attorney General's 2018 speech, the Cyber Law Toolkit and Tallinn-based positions all treat as prohibited intervention?
options: Manipulating another state's electoral system to alter an election result
Copying emails from a foreign ministry for intelligence
Scanning another state's internet address space
Wiping laptops in a ministry without any coercive aim
explain: Wright gave election manipulation as a clear example of intervention, and the Toolkit lists the conduct of elections among protected matters. Espionage and scanning are the least settled cases; a non-coercive wipe is argued under sovereignty, not intervention.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Responses: naming, indictments, sanctions and disruption
question: Officers indicted by the US are very unlikely ever to stand trial. Why do governments still indict them?
options: Because an indictment automatically triggers UN sanctions
Because foreign governments must then extradite their officers
Because indictments are needed before any public attribution
Indictments publish detailed evidence, restrict the defendants' travel, give defenders details to hunt with, and show the operators are known by name
explain: The benefits are evidence, travel risk, defensive value and signalling. Indictments do not trigger UN sanctions or force extradition, and governments often attribute publicly long before any charges.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Threat-informed defence: from a state threat to your detections
question: Your coverage table shows four gaps. Which should normally go first?
options: The technique used by every relevant group that you can neither detect nor mitigate
The technique with the highest ATT&CK id number
The technique most recently added to ATT&CK
Whichever technique is easiest to write a rule for, regardless of use
explain: Prioritise by relevance and exposure: a behaviour shared by all the groups you care about and currently invisible is the biggest risk. ID numbers and recency say nothing about risk; easy rules are fine to do too, but not first by default.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
question: A teammate proposes letting each of the 16 heads in an NSA GQA group keep its own top-16 blocks, arguing it is more accurate. What is the main cost?
options: The backward pass becomes non-differentiable
Decoding would load the union of up to 256 blocks per group instead of 16, losing most of the memory savings
Compression would no longer work
The window branch would have to grow to compensate
explain: Heads in a group share KV, so separate selections are loaded as a union. With 16 heads x 16 blocks that can be up to 256 distinct blocks. Summing scores over the group and taking one top-16 keeps reads at 16 blocks while every head uses all of them.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Where NSA sits: fixed patterns, routing, MoBA and InfLLM-v2
question: A team adds MoBA-style block selection to a dense GQA model with 8 query heads per KV head, each head choosing its own top-4 blocks by mean-pooled keys. Decode latency barely improves. What should they change first?
options: Use a larger block size
Replace mean pooling with an MLP
Make the heads of each group share one selection, for example by summing or averaging their block scores as NSA and InfLLM-v2 do
Turn off the forced current block
explain: Decoding is memory bound, and heads in a group share one KV cache, so independent picks load the union of up to 32 blocks. Summing (NSA) or averaging (InfLLM-v2) scores over the group and taking one top-4 keeps loads at 4 blocks. Block size and scoring function do not fix the union problem.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
question: With 64-bit hashes, m = 4 substrings and threshold r = 7, what is the per-substring search radius that guarantees no match within 7 is missed?
explain: floor(7/4) = 1. If all four substrings differed by 2 or more, the total would be at least 8 > 7, so some substring differs by at most 1. Using 0 could miss pairs such as 2+2+2+1; using 7 is correct but wastes thousands of probes per table.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: The three contracts: policy, generation and environment interfaces
question: Why do generation backends in NeMo RL exchange token ids rather than strings with the trainer?
options: Token ids compress better over NCCL
vLLM cannot return text
Strings cannot be stored in a BatchedDataDict
So the trainer and the inference engine can never disagree because of different tokenizer versions or settings
explain: The generation design doc says backends process tokens directly without involving the tokenizer, which removes inconsistencies between tokenizer versions or specifications in the two frameworks. The log-probs the trainer recomputes are then for exactly the tokens that were sampled.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
question: Async GRPO runs with max_trajectory_age_steps: 1. At training step 7 the buffer still holds a group generated with weights v5. What happens to it?
options: It is evicted: at step 7 only versions 6 and 7 are within the age window
It trains at step 7 with an importance weight to correct it
It waits in the buffer until step 8
The trainer stalls until it is regenerated with v7
explain: The minimum valid version is the current step minus max_trajectory_age_steps, 7 - 1 = 6. ReplayBuffer.sample evicts anything older, so the importance weight only ever corrects up to one step of staleness here.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
question: Your office uses only switches, no hubs. A colleague says sniffing is therefore impossible on the office LAN. What is the best reply?
options: Wrong, because switches copy every frame to a monitoring port by default
Wrong: broadcasts and unknown destinations are flooded, table overflow can force flooding, and ARP or DHCP tricks can redirect frames to an attacker
Wrong, but only for Wi-Fi users
Correct: switches send each frame only to its destination port
explain: Switching reduces what a sniffer sees but does not stop a local attacker. Flooding, MAC table overflow and redirection attacks all deliver other people's frames to the attacker's port. Mirror ports exist but are configured by administrators, not on by default.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Kaminsky 2008: poisoning a whole domain
question: Why did Kaminsky's attack use names like www12345678.bank.example instead of www.bank.example?
options: A name that is not cached forces a new query to the real server at once, so the attacker can race again immediately instead of waiting for a TTL
Random names are shorter, so forged packets are smaller
Random names bypass bailiwick checking
Resolvers do not check query IDs for random names
explain: The whole speed-up comes from always asking for an uncached name. Each one opens a fresh window, so attempts are limited only by how fast the attacker can send, not by record TTLs.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: SYN floods and SYN cookies
question: Why do SYN floods usually use spoofed source addresses, and why does that matter for SYN cookies?
options: Spoofed sources never send the final ACK, so their entries sit in the backlog; with cookies there is no entry, and no ACK means no work
Spoofing makes packets smaller; cookies need small packets
Spoofed addresses bypass the firewall; cookies re-enable it
Spoofing is required by TCP; cookies remove the requirement
explain: The flood works because each SYN creates state that waits for an ACK that never comes. SYN cookies create no state, and the only thing that creates a connection is a correct ACK, which a spoofing attacker never sees the SYN-ACK to compute.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Scanning, as defenders see it
question: A closed port and a filtered port are probed with a SYN. How do they differ in Zeek's conn.log?
options: Closed: history S, state S0. Filtered: history Sr, state REJ.
Closed: history Sr, state REJ. Filtered: history S, state S0.
Both show ShR
Zeek does not log either
explain: A closed port answers with RST (lower-case r, from the responder), which Zeek records as REJ. A filtered port gives no answer at all, which is S0, a connection attempt with no reply.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Packets, flows and logs: three kinds of network evidence
question: A team wants to detect a workstation uploading 5 GB to an unknown server at night, across 4,000 hosts, cheaply, and keep a year of history. Which evidence fits best?
options: Flow records or Zeek conn.log, which record bytes per connection
Full packet capture on every link, kept for a year
Suricata alerts only, since a rule will match the upload
Wireshark running on the analyst's laptop
explain: Volume questions need byte counts per connection, which flows and conn.log record in a few hundred bytes per connection. A year of full packets for 4,000 hosts is enormous. A Suricata rule only fires if someone wrote a rule for this traffic, and a laptop running Wireshark sees only its own traffic.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
question: A stream to TCP port 8443 shows in Wireshark only as 'Data', but the bytes start with 'GET /update HTTP/1.1'. What is the right next step?
options: Use Decode As to dissect TCP port 8443 as HTTP, then read the requests
Conclude the traffic is encrypted
Delete the packets because Wireshark cannot read them
Re-capture with a larger snapshot length
explain: Wireshark chose no HTTP dissector because 8443 is not a port it maps to plain HTTP and no heuristic matched. The payload is plainly HTTP, so Decode As fixes the dissection. The user guide gives the same example with HTTP on port 800.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
question: Why does JA3 drop GREASE values before hashing?
options: Browsers insert randomly chosen GREASE values, so keeping them would give the same browser a different fingerprint on each connection
They are encrypted and cannot be read
GREASE values only appear in server hellos
RFC 8701 forbids logging them
explain: GREASE (RFC 8701) reserves values like 0x0a0a that clients add at random to keep servers tolerant of unknown values. They carry no information about the client, and keeping them would make one browser look like many. The JA3 README says it ignores them so programs that use GREASE still produce a single hash.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: DNS as a control channel: tunnels, generated names and SUNBURST
question: Your Zeek sensor sits on the internet link, outside the internal DNS resolver. A DNS tunnel runs from one workstation. What does dns.log show as the client?
options: The internal resolver's IP address, because the resolver makes the outbound query on the client's behalf
The workstation's IP address
The attacker's IP address
Nothing, because Zeek ignores recursive queries
explain: The workstation asks the internal resolver, which asks the internet. A sensor outside sees only the resolver's queries, so every tunnelled name appears to come from it. Log at the resolver itself or monitor the client side to attribute queries to hosts.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Layers: the OSI and TCP/IP models, and why both exist
question: A vendor sells a 'layer 7 firewall'. What can it do that a firewall that only reads IP addresses and ports cannot?
options: Block traffic from a list of IP addresses
Inspect the application protocol, for example tell a normal HTTP request from one with an attack string in it
Forward Ethernet frames between switch ports
Encrypt the traffic between two offices
explain: Layer 7 is the application layer, so the device parses HTTP, DNS and so on. Blocking by IP address is a layer 3 job any packet filter can do; forwarding frames is layer 2 switching; encrypting between offices is a VPN.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
question: traceroute shows the routers on the path to a host. Which mechanism makes each router reveal itself?
options: Routers answer a special 'who are you' broadcast
Each probe has a TTL one higher than the last; the router where it reaches zero sends back ICMP time exceeded from its own address
BGP announcements list every router on the path
The destination host sends back a list of routers it was reached through
explain: TTL is a hop counter for loop protection. A router that decrements it to zero must drop the packet and may send an ICMP time exceeded message, whose source address is the router itself. traceroute raises the TTL step by step to collect one router per step.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTP: requests, responses, headers and cookies
question: A session cookie is set with `HttpOnly` but not `Secure`, and the site is also reachable over plain HTTP. What risk remains?
options: Scripts in the page can read the cookie
The cookie is sent to every other website
None, HttpOnly covers both cases
The browser may send the cookie over an unencrypted connection, where anyone on the path can read it
explain: HttpOnly only hides the cookie from page scripts. Without Secure, the browser will include it on plain http:// requests to the site, and those cross the network in clear text. Set both, and serve the site only over HTTPS.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
question: A server allocates a large buffer pool at startup and fills it from a single loader thread. Benchmarks show workers on node 1 are slower than workers on node 0. Which change fixes placement with the least code?
options: Call malloc from each worker thread instead of the loader
Add a read-only warm-up pass on each worker after loading
Increase the size of the pool so it spans both nodes
Have each pinned worker write its own share of the pool during startup
