explain: Only revocation makes every existing copy useless. History rewriting leaves clones and forks untouched, narrowing access does nothing about copies already taken, and .gitignore only stops future additions of untracked files.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Splitting a key between people: Shamir's secret sharing
question: A key is split 3-of-5. Two share holders collude. What can they learn about the key?
options: Two thirds of its bits
Nothing: every possible key is equally consistent with two shares
The key, if they also know the prime
Whether the key is even or odd
explain: With k - 1 points, each candidate secret fits exactly one polynomial, so all values remain equally likely. The prime and the scheme are public (Kerckhoffs's principle); the security is in the random coefficients.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: HSMs and PKCS#11: keys that never leave the hardware
question: In PKCS#11, a key object has `CKA_SENSITIVE` set to true. An administrator wants to set it back to false to back the key up in plaintext. What does the standard allow?
options: Any SO can change it back
It can be changed only during a key ceremony
It cannot be changed from true to false
Only on removable tokens
explain: The specification says the attribute can be changed from false to true but not the other way, and CKA_ALWAYS_SENSITIVE records whether it was ever false. Backups of such keys go through wrapping by another key, never plaintext export.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: The end state: workload identity instead of stored secrets
question: Why does SPIFFE prefer X.509-SVIDs over JWT-SVIDs where possible?
options: JWTs cannot carry a SPIFFE ID
A JWT captured in transit can be replayed to impersonate the workload, while an X.509-SVID proves possession of a private key in a TLS handshake
X.509 certificates never expire
JWTs need a vault
explain: The SPIFFE concepts page says tokens are susceptible to replay; with X.509 the private key never travels. JWT-SVIDs still exist for cases such as an application-layer (L7) proxy sitting between workloads.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
question: Which change most directly prevents prototype pollution in a function that copies user-supplied nested JSON into a config object?
options: Build the config with Object.create(null) and skip __proto__, constructor and prototype keys
Validate that the request body is valid JSON before merging
Freeze the user object after merging
Run the merge inside a try/catch block
explain: JSON.parse happily produces a __proto__ key, so valid JSON is not safe JSON. Freezing the result or catching errors happens after Object.prototype was already changed. Null-prototype targets plus refusing the three special keys stop the walk into a prototype.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: ignored errors, text/template and Go's review tools
question: A Go handler renders a user's display name with `html/template`, but the diff wraps the name in `template.HTML(name)` 'so emoji render correctly'. What is the finding?
options: template.HTML marks the string as trusted HTML, so html/template will not escape it, reintroducing XSS
None: html/template escapes everything
It will fail to compile
It only affects text/template
explain: template.HTML is the explicit way to tell html/template a value is already safe markup. Applying it to user data switches off the contextual escaping that made html/template safe. Emoji render fine without it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Compiler warnings and hardening flags a C reviewer should demand
question: A pull request titled 'silence noisy warnings' adds `-Wno-implicit-fallthrough` to the build. What should the reviewer ask for?
options: The list of switch statements that warned, each fixed with a break or marked as intentional fall-through
Nothing: fall-through warnings are style only
Replace it with -w to silence all warnings
Move the flag to the release build only
explain: Each warning is a switch where a missing break may give one case another's behaviour, as role_level showed. Intentional fall-through can be annotated so the warning stays on for new code. Silencing all warnings hides the next goto fail.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: White-box review of a small app, end to end
question: After fixing /search, a teammate says the owner filter in the query means SQL injection could never have leaked other users' notes anyway. What does the probe show?
options: The injected OR 1=1 made the WHERE clause true for every row, and -- commented out the rest, so all notes matched
They are right: the owner filter always applies
The leak came from the attachment endpoint
SQLite ignores the owner column
explain: With q = ' OR 1=1 --, the query became owner = 'ana' AND body LIKE '%' OR 1=1, and the trailing %' was commented out. AND binds tighter than OR, so 1=1 matched every row: the probe returned ids 1 and 2. Injection rewrites the very filter meant to protect the data.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: ESP up close: sequence numbers and the anti-replay window
question: Why must the receiver check the ICV before moving the window?
options: Because checking the ICV is faster than updating the window
Otherwise a forged packet with a very high sequence number could move the window and cause genuine packets to be rejected as too old
Because the ICV contains the window size
It does not matter; RFC 4303 lets implementations choose either order
explain: Moving the window on an unverified packet lets anyone advance it. RFC 4303 states that the receive window is updated only if the integrity verification succeeds.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Inside WireGuard's handshake: Noise IK, four DH results and cookies
question: Why does WireGuard not answer packets with an invalid mac1?
options: To save bandwidth on busy servers
Because mac1 carries the session key
Because UDP cannot carry replies
So that scanners that do not know the server's public key get no response and cannot even confirm the service exists
explain: mac1 is keyed with the responder's public key, so only senders who know whom they are addressing can elicit any reply. The paper calls this "silence is a virtue": no state and no response for unauthenticated packets.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Blast-RADIUS (CVE-2024-3596): MD5 collisions turn Reject into Accept
question: Why does appending the shared secret at the end of the hashed data fail to stop the collision?
options: Because the secret is sent in the clear
Because MD5 ignores the last 16 bytes of its input
Because once two equal-length inputs reach the same MD5 internal state, any identical suffix, including the secret, produces the same final hash
Because the NAS does not know the secret
explain: MD5 is iterative: its output depends only on the internal state and the remaining input. The attacker makes the states equal before the secret is processed, so the unknown suffix cannot separate them. The code example shows this with a real collision.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: VPN leaks and TunnelVision (CVE-2024-3661): routes beat tunnels
question: A laptop's VPN installs 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1 via tun0. A DHCP server pushes 0.0.0.0/1 and 128.0.0.0/1 via the cafe gateway on wlan0. Which statement is right?
options: The VPN routes always win because the VPN installed them first
DHCP cannot install routes that overlap a VPN's routes
The traffic is dropped because the routes conflict
Both sets have the same prefix length, so the tie is broken by route metric or order, an unreliable defence; pushing /2 routes would win outright
explain: Longest prefix wins, and equal lengths fall to secondary rules like metrics, which vary by operating system. An attacker who wants certainty pushes routes more specific than the VPN's. That is why the fix is isolation (namespaces or firewall), not route tricks.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
question: A browser's renderer runs at low integrity on Windows and tries to write a file in the user's Documents folder, which has no integrity label. What happens?
options: The write succeeds because the user owns Documents
The write succeeds but is logged
The renderer's level rises to medium so it can write
The write is refused, because unlabelled objects count as medium and no-write-up applies first
explain: Objects without a label are treated as medium, and the default policy forbids writing up. The integrity check runs before the ordinary permission check, so ownership does not help. Levels never rise automatically.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The perimeter model, Operation Aurora and the road to BeyondCorp
question: Why can BeyondCorp list internal applications in public DNS without weakening security?
options: Because DNS records are encrypted
Because the names are random
Because the access proxy checks user and device on every request, so knowing the name grants nothing
Because Google's DNS servers refuse queries from outside
explain: This is open design: protection rests on the proxy's checks, not on secrecy of names. The record is ordinary public DNS, the name is readable (codereview), and anyone can query it, as the dig output shows.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA versus the VPN
question: Why must the application check the token's `aud` claim, not only its signature?
options: Because the signature alone does not prove the token was meant for this application; a valid token for another back end would also verify
Because `aud` contains the user's password hash
Because without `aud` the token cannot be decoded
Because the signature covers only the header
explain: Every app behind the same proxy sees tokens signed by the same keys. The audience binds a token to one back end, so a token captured by, or issued for, another application is rejected, as the lab's InvalidAudienceError shows.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Measuring the journey: CISA's maturity model and a migration plan
question: According to SP 800-207's migration steps, what should an organisation do before formulating policies for its first zero trust candidate?
options: Buy a ZTNA product
Identify its actors, its assets and its key business processes with their risks
Turn off the VPN
Reach the Optimal stage in the identity pillar
explain: Policies need something to talk about: who the subjects are, what the resources are, and which processes matter most. Buying a product or turning off the VPN first is how migrations break real work.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Queues: acknowledge fast, process later, expect duplicates
question: Why does a dead-letter queue matter for security, not only for reliability?
options: It encrypts messages that failed
A crafted event that crashes the parser would otherwise be retried forever and stall the pipeline; the DLQ isolates it and keeps it as evidence
It stops attackers sending webhooks
It guarantees exactly-once processing
explain: Attackers write some of the fields your pipeline parses. A DLQ bounds the damage of a poison message and preserves it for analysis. It does not encrypt, authenticate or deduplicate anything.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Testing and running automations: dry runs, caps and staged rollout
question: What is shadow mode for?
options: Running the playbook only at night
Hiding automation actions from attackers
Testing against synthetic events only
Running a new playbook on live events without acting, and comparing its proposed actions with what analysts decided
explain: Shadow mode measures a playbook on real traffic at zero risk. Its disagreements with analysts become test cases and evidence for turning actions on.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: AI for finding bugs, reviewing code and writing detections
question: The drafted rule parses as YAML and matches 0 of 3 malicious samples. What is the most dangerous outcome if it is deployed unchecked?
options: The SIEM rejects it at load time
It never fires, and the silence looks like an absence of attacks
It floods analysts with false positives
It slows down the SIEM
explain: Depending on the backend, an unknown field may raise an error or may simply never match. The second is the dangerous one: nothing errors and nothing alerts. Sample-based tests catch it before deployment.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
question: Your web server also runs a database that only the web app on the same machine uses. Which `ss` line would worry you?
options: LISTEN on 0.0.0.0:80
LISTEN on 0.0.0.0:5432
No line for port 5432 at all
explain: 0.0.0.0 means the database accepts connections from any network the machine is on, which adds a door nobody needs. 127.0.0.1 keeps it local. Port 80 is the web server, which is meant to be reachable.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
question: What made WannaCry spread so much faster than ordinary ransomware sent by email?
options: It used a zero-day that no patch could fix
It encrypted files faster
It exploited a network service directly, so each infected machine infected others with no user action
It targeted only hospitals
explain: The SMBv1 bug was reachable over the network without authentication, so WannaCry behaved like a worm. MS17-010 had already fixed it, so it was not a zero-day for patched systems.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Who does security work: the job families
question: A company hires people to break into its own systems, with written permission, so the defenders can practise. What is this group called in NIST's terms?
options: A blue team
A GRC team
A red team
A CNA
explain: NIST defines a red team as a group authorised to emulate a potential adversary's attack. The blue team defends against it.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Maturity models: measuring where you are with C2M2 levels
question: A director asks why the target profile is not MIL3 in every domain. Best answer?
options: Because the auditors would object
Because MIL3 everywhere would cost more than the risk reduction it buys in low-impact domains; targets follow business importance, as C2M2 itself recommends
Because MIL3 cannot be reached by any company
Because C2M2 forbids MIL3 outside the energy sector
explain: C2M2 states that the highest MIL in all domains may not be optimal and that costs should be weighed against benefits. MIL3 is reachable, and the model is not limited to energy.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Reporting to the board: oversight duties and the annual cycle
question: Under NYDFS 500.4(b), which item must the CISO's annual written report cover, to the extent applicable?
options: Plans for remediating material inadequacies
Each employee's training score
The vendor list with prices
Every alert from the year
explain: The section lists confidentiality and integrity, policies, material risks, overall effectiveness, material events and plans for remediating material inadequacies. Operational detail is not required and rarely helps oversight.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Leading through a major incident: the executive layer
question: What is the main purpose of a decision log during a crisis?
options: To record who decided what, on what information and assumptions, so decisions can be revisited, handed over and later explained honestly
To slow decisions down
To replace the incident timeline
To meet a SOC 2 requirement
explain: A decision log makes uncertainty explicit and decisions reviewable. It is also the best defence against later claims that something was hidden, because it shows what was known at the time.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on
question: Which sentence follows the plain language guidance best for a message to a service owner?
options: Your login service accepts expired session tokens; please deploy the fix in pull request 812 by Wednesday.
It is recommended that remediation of the identified issue be performed in a timely manner.
Remediation should be considered by the relevant stakeholders.
A potential weakness may exist in some authentication components.
explain: It is active, present tense, names the system, the defect, the action and the deadline. The others are passive, use hidden verbs ('remediation be performed') and leave out who and when.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
question: Which sentence belongs in an executive summary?
options: An attacker on the internet can take control of the main firewall; the vendor fix takes about an hour to apply and should be applied today.
We used Nmap 7.95 and Burp Suite to enumerate the attack surface.
CVE-2024-3400 was observed on the edge firewall.
The team worked hard over two weeks.
explain: It states the consequence in business terms, the cost of fixing it and the urgency. Tool names, bare CVE numbers and effort statements belong elsewhere or nowhere.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Design-review and code-review comments that get acted on
question: Which review comment is most likely to get a correct fix quickly?
options: issue (security, blocking): /export joins a user-supplied path to the reports directory, so ../ can reach other files. Could we resolve it and check it stays inside? Helper: docs/safe-paths.md
Insecure. Fix.
Why would anyone build it like this?
nitpick: path handling
explain: It is labelled and blocking, locates the defect, gives the scenario, proposes a specific fix and points to a helper. The others give no reason, attack the author, or understate a real issue as a nitpick.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: Why does training the policy head on MCTS visit counts improve the network instead of just copying it?
options: Visit counts are smoother than the prior, so the cross-entropy loss is lower
The search samples at a higher temperature, so the targets are more diverse
The search mixes the prior with measured look-ahead values, so the visit counts differ from the prior where look-ahead finds better moves
The visit counts include moves from human expert games
explain: The search is an improvement operator: it starts from the prior and moves visits toward moves whose measured values are higher. In the toy, the prior said 0.30 for b and the search said 0.889. Imitating that difference is the improvement. AlphaZero uses no human games.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: When the filter lies: lucky answers, proxy rewards, overfitting
question: For which task would a STaR-style final-answer filter keep the fewest flawed rationales, for the same model accuracy?
options: True or false questions
5-way multiple choice questions
Competition math problems with an integer answer
Open-ended summaries scored by a learned reward model
explain: The flawed share depends on c, the chance a flawed attempt matches anyway. It is 0.5 for true or false, 0.2 for 5 options, and tiny for an integer answer. A learned reward model adds its own errors on top, as ReST's human evaluation showed.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
question: In R-Zero, the Solver answers a new question 10 times. Which outcome puts the question in the Solver's training set?
options: 10 of 10 answers agree, so the label is surely right
1 of 10 agree, the hardest kind of question
5 of 10 agree, inside the 3 to 7 band
Any outcome, as long as a Python executor validates the question
explain: R-Zero keeps a question only if 3 to 7 of the 10 answers match the majority-vote pseudo-label: not trivially easy, and not so uncertain that the majority answer is likely to be wrong. There is no executor; the label is the model's own vote.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: Which of the two can return an answer that is wrong for the current question even though the model would have answered correctly?
options: Provider prompt caching
Neither, since both check the full prompt
Semantic caching
Both equally
explain: Prompt caching only skips recomputing an identical prefix; the answer is still generated for the full current prompt. A semantic cache returns an answer generated for a different prompt, and a false hit is exactly that failure.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: LLMLingua step by step: budgets, iterative compression and alignment
question: In the GPT-2 run with iterative_size=200, the end of the prompt came out uncompressed while the start was cut hard. What would you check first?
options: Whether GPT-2 can read numbers
Whether the tail is shorter than one compression window, which our run left untouched, and try a smaller iterative_size
Whether the target LLM supports long prompts
Whether the tokenizer is cl100k
explain: The library compresses window by window; in this run the last part, shorter than a 200-token window, was not compressed. Using 100, the paper's segment size, compressed it. Always inspect the compressed output, not only the ratio.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: SSRF: making the server send your request
question: Which input is the root cause in every SSRF?
options: A user-supplied value that decides the destination (scheme, host or port) of a request the server sends
Any HTTP request that contains a URL in its body
A missing CSRF token
An outdated TLS version
explain: SSRF exists when user input controls where the server connects. A URL in a request body is harmless if the server never fetches it, and CSRF tokens protect browsers, not server-side fetches.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: XML, entities and XXE
question: An image service accepts PNG and JPEG uploads and also, through its imaging library, SVG. Why does that matter for XXE?
options: SVG files are always larger
SVG is XML, so the library may run an XML parser with entity support on user-supplied files
SVG cannot contain text
Browsers block SVG
explain: SVG is an XML format. If the imaging library accepts it, user uploads reach an XML parser, which is hidden XXE attack surface even though the API never mentions XML. Restrict accepted formats and harden the parser.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
question: Equifax had the Struts patch for 67 days before the attackers broke in. According to the House report, which failure also let the attack run for 76 days unseen?
options: No firewall at all
Equifax used Log4j
The attackers used IMDSv1
An expired certificate left the device that inspected ACIS traffic inactive for 19 months
explain: The device that monitored ACIS traffic was inactive while its certificate was expired. When it was renewed on 29 July 2017, suspicious traffic was spotted immediately. Monitoring that silently stops working is a classic failure.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Detecting server-side attacks and the defence map
question: CloudTrail shows the EC2 role of your image-resizing service listing S3 buckets from an IP address outside AWS. What does this most likely mean?
options: Normal behaviour for resizing images
CloudTrail is misconfigured
The bucket is public
The instance's temporary credentials were stolen, for example via SSRF to the metadata service, and are being used elsewhere
explain: Instance role credentials should only be used from the instance. Use from an external IP is what GuardDuty's InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding flags. Revoke the role's sessions, find the SSRF, and check what was read.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
question: With the overlap scheduler on, SGLang launches the forward pass of a grammar request's step k+1 before step k's token has been processed, but holds back its sampling. Why that split?
options: The forward pass does not depend on the grammar, but the mask for k+1 needs the automaton advanced by step k's token
Sampling is slower than the forward pass, so it must be delayed to balance the GPU
The grammar must be recompiled after every token
Tensor-parallel ranks cannot run sampling at the same time
explain: Logits for step k+1 only need the input token, which the GPU already has. The mask, though, is a function of the grammar state after accepting step k's token, which happens on the CPU while the forward pass runs. Delaying only the sampling keeps the overlap and keeps masks correct.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Turning a road map into a weighted directed graph
question: An OSM way is tagged `oneway=yes` and runs from node u to node v. How does it appear in a directed road graph such as an OSMnx MultiDiGraph?
options: As two arcs, u to v and v to u, with the second marked as forbidden
As an undirected edge with a flag that routing code checks
As a single arc from u to v
It is dropped, because one-way streets cannot be routed
explain: Direction is encoded in the graph itself: a one-way street contributes only the arc u to v, while a two-way street contributes two reciprocal arcs. The search then simply never finds a way to travel v to u on that street.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: Your service ingests new traffic speeds every few minutes and must route with them right away. Which OSRM setup fits the docs' guidance?
options: MLD: partition once, rerun osrm-customize with the new speed file
CH, rerunning osrm-contract every few minutes
Plain Dijkstra with no preprocessing
CH with osrm-customize
explain: osrm-customize applies speed and turn-penalty files to a partitioned MLD graph and can be rerun without re-partitioning. CH's contraction would have to be redone, and osrm-customize is not part of the CH pipeline. Plain Dijkstra is far too slow at continental scale.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Convolution, the convolution theorem and FIR filters
question: You compute `ifft(fft(x) * fft(h, len(x)))` to convolve a 1000-sample signal with a 50-tap kernel, and the first 49 output samples look wrong. Why?
options: The FFT is only approximate for lengths that are not powers of two
The DFT product gives circular convolution, so the tail of the output wrapped around onto the start
The kernel must be reversed before the FFT
fft(h, len(x)) truncates the kernel
explain: Multiplying DFTs is circular convolution. The full linear result has 1000 + 50 - 1 = 1049 samples; with only 1000 bins the last 49 wrap onto the first 49. Zero-pad both to at least 1049 (scipy.signal.fftconvolve does this for you).

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
question: Using the model with t_c = 0.54 ns, b = 12 bytes, BW = 30 GB/s, what is the best speedup any lane count can give?
options: About 4x
About 16x
About 1.35x
Unlimited
explain: The memory term is 12 / 30 = 0.4 ns per element and scalar compute is 0.54 ns. With infinite lanes time drops to 0.4 ns, so the speedup is at most 0.54 / 0.4 = 1.35x.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
question: In the last scene, 32 bytes are free yet a 32-byte request fails. Which term names this problem?
options: Internal fragmentation, because the blocks are too large for their contents
External fragmentation, because the free space is split into holes smaller than the request
A memory leak, because B and D were never returned to the allocator
Alignment padding, because 32-byte blocks must start on a 32-byte boundary
explain: B and D were freed correctly, so it is not a leak. The free bytes exist but are scattered into two 16-byte holes, which is external fragmentation. Internal fragmentation is waste *inside* a handed-out block.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
question: A driver calls `kmalloc(260)` a million times. Roughly how much memory is lost to size-class rounding, and what is the usual fix?
options: About 0.25 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 512; give the type its own kmem_cache
Nothing, because kmalloc returns exactly the requested size
About 0.06 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 320; use vmalloc instead
About 0.5 GB lost, since 260 rounds to 1024; allocate whole pages with alloc_pages
explain: The classes go 256 then 512, so each 260-byte request occupies 512 bytes: 252 bytes x 1,000,000 = 252 MB, about 0.25 GB. A dedicated cache sized for the object (kmem_cache_create) removes almost all of that waste.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4
question: After switching an MoE run to an INT4 rollout checkpoint, rewards collapse right after the first weight update and `--check-weight-update-equal` reports the router weights as all zeros on the SGLang side. What is the most likely cause?
options: The KV cache is in FP8
The checkpoint's quantization ignore list does not cover `mlp.gate`, so the router was quantized and then skipped by SGLang
--sglang-mem-fraction-static is too high
Megatron cannot train INT4 models
explain: The debug guide describes exactly this: the router weight is a plain 2D tensor but not a Linear layer. Without an ignore entry such as `re:.*mlp\.gate\..*` it is quantized online, SGLang does not load quantized router names, and the router stays zero.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Is the run working? Evaluation, metrics, checkpoints and recovery
question: A run with `--save-interval 50`, straw transport and no epoch boundary nearby dies while training rollout 340. You resubmit to the same Ray cluster. Where does training resume, and what is lost?
options: From the checkpoint saved after rollout 299; the batches from 300 on are retrained from retained straw data, so no generated samples are lost
From rollout 340, because the engines kept their weights
From the checkpoint after rollout 300; batch 340 is regenerated
From the beginning, because the optimizer state is not saved
explain: Saves happen after rollout r when r + 1 is a multiple of 50, so the last one followed rollout 299. The new trainer loads it and retrains every batch after it, including batches that finished training but were never saved. straw kept their samples and rewards; only the training compute since the checkpoint is repeated.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Inside the EVM: storage, calls, msg.sender and delegatecall
question: Contract P delegatecalls contract L, and L's code sets slot 0 to 42. Which storage changes?
options: L's slot 0
Both P's and L's slot 0
P's slot 0
Neither: delegatecall is read-only
explain: Delegatecall executes L's code in P's context, so writes land in P's storage. STATICCALL, not DELEGATECALL, is the read-only variant.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Unchecked external calls and denial of service
question: A payroll function loops over every employee in a storage array and pays each with transfer(). Anyone can add themselves to the array. What are the two DoS risks?
options: Integer overflow and signature replay
Reentrancy and front-running
One employee whose receive reverts blocks everyone, and a long array exceeds the block gas limit
There is no risk because transfer() limits gas
explain: transfer() reverts the whole function if any recipient fails (SWC-113), and an attacker-grown loop runs out of gas (SWC-128). Pull payments fix both.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Upgradeable proxies and storage collisions
question: Why does EIP-1967 subtract 1 from the hash when choosing the implementation slot?
options: To make the slot number odd
Because slot numbers start at 1
To fit the value in 255 bits
So nobody knows a preimage of the slot, and a mapping write with a crafted key cannot land on it
explain: Mapping entries live at keccak256-derived slots. EIP-1967 adds the -1 offset so the preimage of the slot cannot be known, which ensures a write to a mapping with a maliciously crafted key could not overwrite it.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Finding bugs early: review, static analysis, fuzzing, formal methods
question: Which question is a static analyser like Slither best suited to answer?
options: Is this oracle's price economically manipulable?
Are the signers' laptops compromised?
Does any function write state after an external call?
Will users like the protocol?
explain: Static analysis matches code patterns such as state written after a call. Economic manipulability and operational security need human review and threat modelling.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Verdicts, severity and priority: true, false and benign positives
question: A rule detects `vssadmin delete shadows`. It fires because the backup product deletes old shadow copies every night at 01:00, exactly as configured. What is the verdict, and what is the fix?
options: False positive; delete the rule
True positive; escalate to incident response
Benign true positive; record the backup schedule and add a narrow, documented exception for that product's signed process at that time
Undetermined; leave it open
explain: The rule saw exactly what it was built to see, so it is not a false positive. The activity is legitimate, so it is not an attack. The fix is context: a narrow exception tied to the backup product, not deleting a rule that catches ransomware precursors.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Malware on an endpoint: reading a process tree
question: Four parent and child pairs appear in today's EDR data. Which deserves the fastest look?
options: explorer.exe starting WINWORD.EXE
explorer.exe starting chrome.exe
explorer.exe starting Teams.exe
WINWORD.EXE starting powershell.exe -EncodedCommand
explain: The first three are a user launching ordinary applications from the desktop. A word processor launching an encoded PowerShell command is a classic sign of a malicious document.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When to escalate, and case notes someone else can act on
question: Which case-note summary lets an incident lead act fastest?
options: "Weird stuff on a laptop, see the logs"
"Malware alert. Ran some queries. Looks bad."
"FIN-LT-042 ran a malicious macro at 09:15 UTC; an unknown device signed in as the user at 09:41. Host isolated, sessions revoked. Need IR to scope the account's access."
A copy of the full raw logs with no summary
explain: It states what happened, when, to what, how sure, what is already done and what is needed. The others force the reader to redo the triage.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
question: A company forces monthly password changes. An audit finds many passwords on sticky notes. What does Adams and Sasse's study suggest is the main cause?
options: Employees are careless and need stricter penalties
Sticky notes are too easy to buy
The policy demands more memorisation than people can manage, so they write passwords down to cope
Monthly changes are too infrequent
explain: Their respondents linked writing passwords down directly to forced changes and to having many passwords. Penalties do not reduce the memory load; changing the policy does.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: A caller claiming to be from IT gives a callback number 'in case we get cut off'. What should the employee do to verify the caller?
options: Call the number given, since that proves the caller answers it
Ask the caller three questions only real IT staff would know
Look up the service desk in the company directory and call that number instead
Check that caller ID shows the company's name
explain: A number supplied by the caller leads back to the caller. Caller ID and display names are set by the caller too. Only a number from a source the caller does not control, such as the directory, verifies anything.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure
question: Which change most reduces the number of risky judgement calls the help desk has to make at all?
options: Longer calls with more personal questions
Self-service recovery that requires an existing strong factor, such as a passkey
Allowing resets by email
Publishing the help desk's verification questions
explain: If most people can recover by proving a factor they still hold, only the rare cases with no factor left reach an agent, and those can get the slow, strong checks.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Badges, readers and tailgating
question: A log shows badge B22 exiting the lab at 08:50 with no entry by B22 that day. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: The badge reader's clock is wrong
B22 cloned someone else's card
B22 followed someone into the lab without badging (tailgating or piggybacking)
B22 works from home
explain: An exit with no matching entry is the classic trace of tailgating. Confirm with CCTV and a conversation, and look at whether the door-held alarm fired around the time B22 must have entered.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: A reporting culture, and what to do when someone is fooled
question: After a tailgater is spotted in a restricted area, what should be preserved first?
options: The visitor sign-in sheet only
Nothing, as the person has left
CCTV footage and badge logs, before they are overwritten
The door hardware
explain: Recordings and logs often roll over after a set period. They show who entered, when, and where they went, including near network ports and unlocked screens.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
question: You compare a 4,096-latent and a 65,536-latent SAE on the same layer. The smaller one has a 'Python code' latent; the larger has several latents for different Python contexts and none that matches it exactly. What does this indicate?
options: The larger SAE is broken
Feature splitting: the wider dictionary covers the same concept at finer resolution
The smaller SAE has dead latents
Python is not represented in the model
explain: This is the expected pattern from Towards Monosemanticity: wider dictionaries refine broad latents into families of more specific ones.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines
question: Your team must flag customer messages that mention cancelling, and has 2,000 labelled examples. Which first approach does the evidence in this lesson support?
options: Search the SAE for a 'cancellation' latent and threshold it, since SAE latents are the model's true units
Train a much wider SAE until a perfect cancellation latent appears
Use raw model outputs only; internal activations cannot be probed
Train a linear probe or a difference-in-means direction on the raw activations, and use SAE latents only if they measurably add to it
explain: With labels available, Kantamneni et al. and AxBench found supervised baselines on raw activations match or beat SAE latents, especially under distribution shift. Wider SAEs absorb more, and SAE latents are not canonical units.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
question: Two sensors sit 10 m apart and read 30 and 31. A third sensor equally far from the target, in another direction, reads 12. Compared with IDW, how will ordinary kriging weight them (assume a range of several km)?
options: Exactly like IDW, because the distances to the target are equal
It gives the pair all the weight because they agree with each other
It gives every sensor weight 1/3 regardless of position
It gives the close pair less weight each, treating them almost like one sensor, and the lone sensor relatively more
explain: The pair is nearly redundant: $\Gamma$ shows they are strongly correlated with each other, so kriging splits roughly one sensor's worth of weight between them. IDW only looks at distance to the target, so it counts the pair twice.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: Draft q = (0.7, 0.3) and target p = (0.4, 0.6) over two tokens {A, B}. The draft proposes A. What is the probability A is kept, and if not, what is sampled?
options: Kept with prob 0.4; otherwise sample from p
Kept with prob 4/7; otherwise output B with probability 1
Kept with prob 0.7; otherwise output B
Always kept, since A has nonzero target probability
explain: Acceptance is min(1, p(A)/q(A)) = 0.4/0.7 = 4/7. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0, 0.3) normalizes to B with probability 1. Check: P(A) = 0.7 x 4/7 = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3 + 0.7 x 3/7 = 0.6.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
question: A tree-attention kernel accidentally uses the ordinary causal mask on the flattened tree. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; causal masking is a superset of tree masking
Only the position ids are off by one
The pass becomes slower but results are identical
Each node also attends to earlier sibling branches, so the target scores tokens in contexts that never occur and verification becomes wrong
explain: Under a causal mask 'think' would attend to 'It', 'is', 'was' and so on, a context that is not its real prefix. Its distribution is then wrong and so are the accept and reject decisions. The mask must restrict attention to ancestors.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
question: Which single change halves the number of spectrogram frames per second?
options: Increase the window from 25 ms to 50 ms
Increase the hop from 10 ms to 20 ms
Reduce the mel bands from 80 to 40
Resample from 16 kHz to 8 kHz but keep a 25 ms window and 10 ms hop
explain: Frames per second is 1 / hop, so a 20 ms hop gives 50 frames per second. A longer window makes each frame cover more time but they still start every 10 ms. Fewer mel bands makes each column shorter, not the sequence. Resampling changes samples per frame, not frames per second.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
question: A clinic transcribes hour-long recordings with long pauses, and reviewers find invented sentences in the quiet parts. Which change targets the cause most directly?
options: Use a larger beam
Run VAD and send only detected speech to the model
Lower the compression-ratio threshold to 1.5
Switch WER normalizers
explain: The invented text appears where there is no speech for the decoder to follow. Removing non-speech before decoding takes away the empty input the decoder fills. A larger beam or a stricter compression threshold targets loops, not fluent inventions, and a normalizer only changes scoring.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
question: A random-access hash table grows from 2 MiB to 512 MiB and slows down more than its cache miss rate explains. Which change most directly targets the extra cost?
options: Use a TLB with twice as many entries
Switch from malloc to calloc
Increase RLIMIT_STACK
Back the table with 2 MiB huge pages (for example madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE))
explain: 512 MiB of random access is far beyond a 4 KiB-page TLB's reach, so most accesses also need a page walk. 2 MiB pages raise reach 512 times, so the table needs only 256 translations. You cannot buy a bigger TLB in software, and the other options do not touch translation.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: What does ActAdd need in order to build a steering vector?
options: A labeled dataset of a few thousand examples and a few gradient steps
A trained linear probe on the target concept
One pair of contrasting prompts and two forward passes
Access to the model's training data
explain: ActAdd is optimization-free: two forward passes on a prompt pair such as Love and Hate, a subtraction, and a scale factor. CAA (lesson 2), ITI (inference-time intervention, developed independently of ActAdd, slightly earlier) and the reading vectors of RepE (representation engineering) use more examples to get a cleaner direction; none of these fine-tunes the model.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Why is a random vector of the same norm a necessary baseline?
options: To check the hook is installed
Because random vectors are always better at steering
To show the effect comes from the direction and not from merely perturbing the stream by that much
To estimate the residual stream norm
explain: Any large perturbation changes outputs somewhat. ActAdd and ITI both compared against random directions (ITI's random direction moved TruthfulQA from 30.5% to only 31.2%) to show their direction specifically carries the concept.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
question: Which timestamp should you use to decide whether a machine overheated between 14:00:00 and 14:00:10?
options: Processing time at the stream processor
Kafka's append time for the record
The event time the sensor stamped on the reading
The time the database row was written
explain: Only the event time refers to when the physical measurement happened. The other three are processing times at different stages, each shifted by network and queueing delay.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
question: A consumer commits its Kafka offset immediately after reading a batch and before writing results. It crashes mid-write. What semantics did you get?
options: Exactly once
At least once
At most once: the batch's unwritten results are lost
No effect, Kafka rolls back the commit
explain: Committing before processing means on restart the consumer resumes after the batch; anything not yet written is never processed. Kafka's docs describe this as the at-most-once pattern.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
question: With d_model = 512, how many parameters are in the four projection matrices (W^Q, W^K, W^V for all heads, plus W^O) of one multi-head attention layer, ignoring biases?
explain: Each of W^Q, W^K, W^V is 8 heads x (512 x 64) = 512 x 512 in total, and W^O is 512 x 512. That gives 4 x 512^2 = 1,048,576 weights. Splitting into heads does not multiply the parameter count.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: A team switches a 24-layer post-LN Transformer to pre-LN. According to Xiong et al. (2020), what change to the training recipe becomes reasonable to try?
options: Removing or shortening the learning-rate warmup stage
Removing the causal mask
Dividing by d_k instead of its square root
Removing positional encodings
explain: Xiong et al. show that post-LN has large expected gradients near the output at initialization, which makes warmup necessary. With LayerNorm inside the residual branch (pre-LN) the gradients are well-behaved and they train without warmup at comparable quality.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25's IDF and a full worked example
question: A colleague's BM25 implementation returns negative scores for the query the cat. What is the most likely cause?
options: A bug in the length normalization
k1 is set too high
Using the RSJ IDF, which is negative for terms in more than half the documents, such as the
avgdl is computed over the wrong field
explain: The term weight is the only factor that can be negative: the TF factor f/(f + K) is always between 0 and 1. With RSJ IDF, a term like the in over half the documents gets a negative weight. Fixes: floor at 0, use Lucene's ln(1 + ...) form, or drop stopwords.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Fields measured, and what is fixed at index time
question: A team runs Lucene's built-in BM25 and wants to try b = 0.5 instead of 0.75 on a live index. What does it take?
options: Only a similarity setting change: k1 and b are applied at query time and the stored norms do not depend on them
A full reindex, because b is baked into every posting
Rebuilding the analyzer
Nothing; b cannot be changed in Lucene
explain: Lucene's BM25 stores term counts and a one-byte length; the scorer builds its table from k1, b and avgdl for each query. Lucene's documentation says its supplied similarities can be swapped at runtime without reindexing. In Elasticsearch the similarity lives in the index settings; its docs say that changing it on an existing index means closing the index, updating the settings and reopening it, still with no reindex.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
question: For GPT-2 small, roughly what share of all parameters sits in the MLPs?
options: About 10%
About 23%
About 45%
About 31%
explain: The MLPs have 8C^2 + 5C per block, twice attention's 4C^2 + 4C, totalling 56.67M of 124.44M, which is 45.5%. 23% is attention and 31% is the token embedding table.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP
question: Which of these changes alters the numbers the model computes, not just how fast it computes them?
options: Switching from manual attention to scaled_dot_product_attention
Moving matmuls from float32 to TF32 or bfloat16
Wrapping the model in DDP with gradients averaged across 8 GPUs
Fusing AdamW into one kernel
explain: Lower-precision formats round the matmul inputs, so results differ slightly from float32; that is the accuracy traded for speed. Fused attention computes the same function (we saw agreement to 7e-7), DDP's averaged gradient equals one big batch's, and a fused optimizer does the same update.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
question: What is the derivative of softplus $\ln(1 + e^z)$ at $z = 0$?
options: 0, because ReLU has slope 0 to the left of 0
1, because softplus is a version of ReLU
0.5, because the slope of softplus is the sigmoid and $\sigma(0) = 0.5$
About 0.693, the value of softplus at 0
explain: The chain rule gives $\zeta'(z) = e^z/(1 + e^z) = \sigma(z)$, and $\sigma(0) = 1/2$. 0.693 is $\ln 2$, the height of softplus at 0, not its slope. Unlike ReLU, softplus has no corner, so its slope at 0 is well defined.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
question: At a critical point the Hessian has eigenvalues 4 and -1. What kind of point is it?
options: A saddle point: the function curves up along one eigenvector and down along the other
A local minimum, because the larger eigenvalue is positive
A local maximum, because one eigenvalue is negative
Cannot tell without the gradient
explain: Mixed signs mean the point is a minimum along one direction and a maximum along another: a saddle. A minimum needs every eigenvalue positive. The gradient is already known to be zero at a critical point, so it adds nothing.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: You type `deploy` and get `command not found` with status 127, yet `ls -l ~/bin/deploy` shows the file exists with mode `-rwxr-xr-x`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file needs a .sh extension
Exit status 127 means the program crashed while starting
`~/bin` is not one of the directories in PATH
Bash only searches PATH for builtins
explain: Names without a slash are only looked up in the PATH directories. Add the directory to PATH or call it by path, `~/bin/deploy`. Extensions mean nothing to the kernel, and a crash would give a different status.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Pipes: concurrent processes, sort | uniq -c, and SIGPIPE
question: Which pipeline lists the 3 most common words in words.txt (one word per line)?
options: `uniq -c words.txt | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3`
`sort -rn words.txt | uniq -c | head -n 3`
`sort words.txt | head -n 3 | uniq -c`
explain: Sort first so equal words are adjacent, count with uniq -c, then sort the counts numerically in reverse and take 3. The third option sorts the words themselves, not counts, and the last one cuts the data before counting.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
question: A batch contains the token IDs [2, 2, 4] and the model uses an embedding table with 5 rows. After one backward pass, which rows of the table have a nonzero gradient?
options: All 5 rows, because the whole matrix is a parameter
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient being the sum of two contributions
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient counted once because duplicates are removed
Only row 4, because repeated tokens cancel out
explain: Only looked-up rows get gradient, and a row looked up twice accumulates both contributions (the lookup's backward pass is a scatter-add: each position's gradient is added into the row its ID points to, so repeats sum). Rows 0, 1 and 3 get exactly zero, which is what makes sparse updates possible.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim
question: You reproduce a skip-gram result with gensim's `Word2Vec`, passing `vector_size=100`, `negative=5` and `ns_exponent=0.75` and leaving every other argument at its default. Your scores do not match the reference. Which setting is most likely wrong?
options: `ns_exponent=0.75`
`negative=5`
`vector_size=100`
`sg` was left at its default 0, so it trained CBOW
explain: With `sg` left at its default 0, gensim trains CBOW, which predicts the center from averaged context vectors. The three settings you passed are valid skip-gram values (5 negatives and the 3/4 exponent are the paper's choices). CBOW is a fine model, but it is a different one, so results will not match a skip-gram reference.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Where word vectors fail: unseen words, many senses and bias
question: A support chatbot built on static word vectors treats *Apple* the fruit and *Apple* the company identically. What does this lesson suggest?
options: Increase the vector dimension so both senses fit
Use contextual embeddings, which compute a separate vector per occurrence
Train with more negative samples
Use hierarchical softmax instead of negative sampling
explain: A static table has one row per word, so every sense shares it whatever the dimension or training objective. Contextual models compute a vector from each sentence, so the two uses differ.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
question: Elementwise operations (add, ReLU, LayerNorm) are at most a few FLOP/B. What is the standard way to make them cheaper on a GPU?
options: Use more Tensor Cores
Fuse them into the neighbouring kernel so the data is not written to and re-read from HBM
Increase the clock speed
Split them across more thread blocks
explain: They are memory-bound, so the only lever is fewer bytes moved. Fusing several elementwise steps into one kernel keeps the intermediate values on chip. More math units do not help a memory-bound operation.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
question: Why does continuous batching improve throughput over static batching?
options: Finished requests free their slot right away and waiting requests join at the next step, so fewer slots sit idle
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache
It runs prefill and decode on different GPUs
explain: The step time is unchanged; what changes is how full the batch is. Iteration-level scheduling refills slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest request.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
question: An `int` holding `0x12345678` is stored at address 0x100 on x86-64. Which byte is at address 0x100?
explain: x86-64 is little-endian: the least significant byte, 0x78, goes at the lowest address, followed by 0x56, 0x34 and 0x12 at 0x101 to 0x103. A big-endian machine would put 0x12 first.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why real CPUs beat the simple loop: pipelines and prediction
question: A profile shows a hot loop whose `if` on input data is mispredicted about half the time. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Add a few more instructions before the if so the CPU has time to think
Make the outcome predictable or branch-free, for example sort or group the data, or let the compiler use a conditional move
Split the loop across two functions
Turn off out-of-order execution
explain: The cost comes from flushing the pipeline on each wrong guess. Removing the guess (a conditional move) or making it right almost every time (sorted or grouped data) removes the penalty. Extra instructions or function boundaries do not make the direction any easier to predict.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
question: Using C of about 6ND, a 7B-parameter model trained on 2 trillion tokens needs roughly how many FLOPs?
explain: 6 x 7e9 x 2e12 = 8.4e22. The rule ignores attention's context-length term, which Kaplan et al. note is small when the model width is large relative to the context.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Policy gradients: how a score becomes a gradient
question: A policy samples response C, which has reward -1, with probabilities p = (0.426, 0.258, 0.316) over A, B, C. Without a baseline, how does this one sample move the three logits under gradient ascent?
options: It raises all three logits, because the gradient of a probability is always positive
It lowers C's logit and raises A's and B's, since r times (onehot(C) - p) = (0.426, 0.258, -0.684)
It raises C's logit, because C was the response sampled
It leaves the logits unchanged, because negative rewards give no gradient
explain: The sample's contribution is r(C) times (onehot(C) - p) = -1 times (-0.426, -0.258, 0.684). Ascent lowers C's logit by the largest amount and lifts the others. A negative reward acts like a push away from what was sampled.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
question: Why does an inverted index keep each postings list sorted by docID?
options: So that the most relevant documents come first
So two lists can be intersected by walking them once, side by side
Because docIDs must be unique
So the dictionary can be binary searched
explain: A single global sort order lets the query engine merge two lists in one linear pass (lesson 4). Sorting by docID says nothing about relevance; ranking is a separate step. Binary search over the dictionary concerns terms, not postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Phrase and proximity queries with a positional index
question: Why can a phrase query on a positional index not finish in O(x + y) steps, where x and y are the two terms' document frequencies, even with skip pointers?
options: For each document both terms share, it must also walk both position lists, so the work grows with the number of occurrences, not documents
Positions break the docID sort order, so the docID merge no longer works
A phrase query must scan every document in the collection
Skip pointers cannot be stored in a positional index
explain: The docID merge (with skips) still works exactly as in lesson 4. The extra cost is inside each shared document: comparing positions costs time proportional to how often the two terms occur there. That is why the textbook bounds positional queries by the token count T instead of the document count N.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
question: `int a = -7, b = 2;` What are `a / b` and `a % b` in C99 and later?
options: -4 and 1
-3 and 1
-3 and -1
explain: Both operands are int, so this is integer division, which truncates toward zero: -3.5 becomes -3, not -4. The remainder must satisfy (a/b)*b + a%b == a, that is -6 + a%b == -7, so a%b is -1. The remainder takes the sign of the left operand.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: A function `void clear(char *buf)` does `memset(buf, 0, sizeof buf);` (memset sets that many bytes to 0) and callers pass a `char buf[256]`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, sizeof buf is 256
It clears only 8 bytes, because buf is a pointer inside the function
It clears 257 bytes including the terminator
It fails to compile because arrays cannot be passed
explain: Inside clear, buf is a char *, so sizeof buf is the pointer size (8 on 64-bit platforms), not 256. The array's size is lost at the call. The fix is `void clear(char *buf, size_t n)` and `memset(buf, 0, n)`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
question: `const char *w[] = {"pear", "fig", "kiwi"};` is sorted with `qsort(w, 3, sizeof w[0], cmp)`. Which cmp is correct?
options: return strcmp(a, b);
return strcmp(*(const char * const *)a, *(const char * const *)b);
return strcmp((const char *)a, (const char *)b);
return *(const char *)a - *(const char *)b;
explain: Each element of w is a `const char *`, so qsort passes a pointer to one: a `const char * const *`. Dereferencing it gives the string. Options 1 and 3 treat the address of the pointer as if it were the characters. Option 4 compares the first bytes of the pointers themselves, not the strings. A test sort with option 2 gave fig kiwi pear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
question: A third-party library, shipped only as a compiled binary, seems to corrupt the heap in your Linux service. You cannot recompile it. Which tool fits first?
options: AddressSanitizer, by adding -fsanitize=address to your own build
Valgrind memcheck on the existing binary
-Wall -Wextra on your own code
gdb with a breakpoint on main
explain: Valgrind instruments the program at run time, including code in libraries you did not compile, so no rebuild is needed. ASan only instruments code compiled with the flag, and warnings only see your source. A debugger helps once you know where to look.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: A colleague says the Vec error is pointless in single-threaded code because no other thread can touch `v`. What is the best reply?
options: They are right; the check only matters with threads
`push` may reallocate and free the old buffer, so `first` could dangle even with one thread
`push` always copies the vector, so `first` becomes stale but still safe to read
explain: Reallocation frees the old block, so the shared reference could point at freed memory: a use after free with no threads involved. `push` only reallocates when length equals capacity, which is exactly why the danger is easy to miss in testing.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
question: A struct holds a borrowed field: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. What does the `'a` promise?
options: The `Parser` lives for the whole program
The `input` string is copied into the `Parser`
A `Parser` value cannot outlive the string data that `input` borrows
The `Parser` owns the string and will drop it
explain: A lifetime parameter on a struct ties the struct's validity to the borrowed data. The struct does not own the string, and nothing is copied. The checker rejects any use of the `Parser` after the borrowed string is dropped.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: A search system ranks documents by raw dot product with the query embedding. Users complain that long, rambling documents always win. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Use more embedding dimensions
Square every dot product before ranking
Add a constant to every component of the query
Rank by cosine similarity, or normalize all embeddings to unit length
explain: If document vectors grow longer with document length, the dot product rewards that length. Dividing by the norms (cosine) keeps only direction. More dimensions or squaring the score keeps the length effect; adding a constant changes the query's direction, not the bias.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
question: $\det A = 3$ and $\det B = -2$ for two $2 \times 2$ matrices. What is $\det(AB)$, and is $AB$ invertible?
options: -6, and AB is invertible
1, and AB is invertible
-6, and AB is not invertible because its determinant is negative
6, and AB is invertible
explain: Determinants multiply under composition: $3 \times (-2) = -6$. Any nonzero determinant means no direction is squashed flat, so $AB$ has an inverse, $B^{-1}A^{-1}$. The sign only records the orientation flip that $B$ introduces.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
question: A colleague removes the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor and raises $d_k$ from 64 to 1024. What do you expect?
options: Nothing changes, because softmax only depends on the ranking of scores
Scores shrink toward 0, so attention becomes uniform
Scores spread about 4 times wider, softmax gets much peakier and training can slow because gradients shrink
The product QK^T becomes undefined
explain: Typical score size grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$: $\sqrt{1024}/\sqrt{64} = 4$. Softmax depends on score *differences*, not just their ranking, so wider scores mean near one-hot weights and tiny gradients. Shapes still match, so nothing errors.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Classification end to end: logistic regression, boundaries and softmax
question: A softmax classifier gives probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) and the correct class is the third. What is the gradient of the loss with respect to the three scores?
explain: The gradient is $p$ minus the one-hot label (0, 0, 1): $(0.7, 0.2, 0.1 - 1) = (0.7, 0.2, -0.9)$. Gradient descent subtracts it, so the wrong classes' scores go down and the correct one goes up, most strongly where the model was most wrong.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
question: A disease screen is positive for 50 of 10,000 patients. Model A has AUC 0.97; at its chosen threshold it flags 500 patients, 45 of them sick. What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 0.97, recall 0.97
Precision 0.09, recall 0.90
Precision 0.90, recall 0.09
Precision 0.45, recall 0.90
explain: Precision = 45/500 = 0.09: 91 percent of flags are false alarms. Recall = 45/50 = 0.90. A high AUC says the model ranks well, not that its flags are mostly right when positives are this rare.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
question: A network has three hidden layers of 512 units each, but every activation is the identity. Which statement is true?
options: It can only represent affine functions of its input, same as a single linear layer
It can represent any continuous function given enough units
It can represent XOR but not more complex functions
It is equivalent to a single hidden layer network with ReLU
explain: Each layer is affine and the composition of affine maps is affine, so the whole stack collapses to $W'x+b'$. The extra parameters add cost but no expressive power.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand
question: A colleague implements BP2 as `d1 = (W2 @ d2) * a1 * (1 - a1)` for a network where W2 has shape (10, 64). What happens?
options: It works, matrix order does not matter
It computes the gradient for the biases instead
It fails or computes garbage: the error must go back through the transpose, W2.T @ d2, giving one value per hidden unit
It only breaks when the batch size is 1
explain: W2 maps 64 hidden units to 10 outputs. Going backward, the 10 output errors must be distributed to 64 hidden units along the same connections: that is $(W^2)^\top \delta^2$, shape 64. W2 @ d2 is a shape error here, and for square matrices it silently produces wrong gradients, which a gradient check would catch.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
question: You train a 10-class classifier and the very first loss printed is 9.7. What does that most likely tell you?
options: Training is going well; high loss means room to improve
The initial logits are far from uniform (for example, weights initialised too large), or the loss is computed wrongly
The dataset has more than 10 classes
The learning rate is too small
explain: With small random weights the logits are nearly equal and the loss should be about $\ln 10 = 2.30$. A much larger value means the network starts out confidently wrong, typically from oversized initial weights, or there is a bug such as applying the loss to the wrong tensor. Check this before training.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
question: In the same 16 KB example, a program touches virtual page 100 (binary 0110 0100). What happens?
options: The hardware reads the PTE at index 4 of the page at frame 100
The PDE at index 6 is invalid, so the hardware raises an exception without reading any page of PTEs
The MMU allocates a new page of PTEs for that region
It maps to frame 100, the first valid entry
explain: The directory index is the top 4 bits, 0110 = 6, and only PDEs 0 and 15 are valid. An invalid PDE means no PTE in that 16-page region is valid, so the access traps right away. Allocating page-table pages is the OS's job, not the MMU's.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
question: A team makes every thread acquire locks in increasing address order. Which deadlock condition does that remove?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold-and-wait
No preemption
Circular wait
explain: Threads still hold locks exclusively, still hold one while waiting for the next, and locks still cannot be taken away. But a cycle would need some thread to hold a higher lock while waiting for a lower one, which the order forbids, so circular wait cannot form.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
question: A crash leaves only the new inode I[v2] on disk; the bitmap B[v2] and data block Db were not written. What is the state?
options: Inconsistent: the inode points to a block the bitmap says is free, and that block holds old garbage
Consistent and correct: the inode is the source of truth
A harmless space leak
Lost data but a consistent file system
explain: The inode now points to the new data block (block 5 in OSTEP), but Db never reached it, so reading the file returns whatever was there before. The bitmap still says that block is free, contradicting the inode. This is the case fsck or journaling exists to prevent. Only-Db is the harmless case; only-bitmap is the leak.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
question: Using the spam table (0.24, 0.06, 0.07, 0.63), what is P(contains free | not spam)?
options: 0.07, the joint cell
0.31, the share of all emails containing free
0.23, which is 70 of the 310 emails containing free
0.10, which is 70 of the 700 non-spam emails
explain: Condition on not spam: take that row (0.07 and 0.63, total 0.70) and divide: 0.07 / 0.70 = 0.10. Option C divides by the wrong total: it is P(not spam | free), the reversed conditional.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
question: Two features in your data have correlation 0. What can you safely conclude?
options: They are independent, so a model gains nothing from using both
They have no linear association, but one may still depend strongly on the other
Their covariance matrix is the identity
One of them is constant
explain: Zero correlation rules out a linear trend only; y = x squared on symmetric x has correlation 0 and full dependence. The covariance matrix is diagonal, but not the identity unless both variances are 1.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
question: Two experiments find the same 0.2 point lift in conversion. Experiment 1 (50,000 users) has p = 0.01; experiment 2 (5,000 users) has p = 0.40. What is the best conclusion?
options: Experiment 2 shows the lift is absent
The experiments contradict each other
Both are consistent with the same lift; experiment 2 is too small to distinguish it from noise
Experiment 1 must have a bug, since the lifts match but p differs
explain: Same effect, ten times fewer users means a standard error about sqrt(10) = 3.2 times larger, so a much smaller z and larger p. A non-significant result is not evidence of no effect; its confidence interval is just wide enough to include 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does loss rise again for the largest models at a fixed budget?
options: Large models overfit any dataset
With compute fixed, a larger N leaves fewer tokens, so the data term B/D^beta grows
Large models have a larger irreducible loss E
Backward passes cost more than forward passes
explain: At fixed C, $D = C/(6N)$. Pushing N up shrinks D, and the finite-data penalty grows faster than the finite-model penalty falls. E is the same for every model, and the 6N cost is already accounted for in the budget.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Batch size, learning rate and data limits as you scale
question: You have 300B unique tokens and compute for 3T tokens of training (10 epochs). Which plan does data-constrained scaling favour?
options: Repeat the data on a model somewhat smaller than the fresh-data optimum, accepting that later epochs are worth less
Train once on 300B tokens and leave 90 percent of the compute unused, since repeated data is worthless
Train a 10x larger model on one epoch, since extra parameters keep their full value
Use the fresh-data optimal model for 3T tokens, since repeats are exactly as good as fresh data
explain: At 10 epochs $D' \approx 7.8\,U_D$: repeats still add a lot, but less than fresh data would. Excess parameters decay faster than repeated data ($R_N^{*} \approx 5.3$ against $R_D^{*} \approx 15.4$), so the optimum shifts toward a smaller model on more epochs. Repeats are not worthless before roughly 40 epochs.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
question: A query has exactly 3 relevant documents in the qrels. A perfect system ranks all 3 first. What are its P@10 and R@10?
explain: Recall is 3/3 = 1.0 because every relevant document is retrieved. Precision at 10 counts all 10 slots, and only 3 can ever be relevant, so it is 0.3 even for a perfect ranking. This is why P@k is hard to average across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.
